📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • Sources indicate that cyclists, myself included, are often data driven.
  • Sources indicate that many riders and multisport athletes just don’t need a dedicated bike computer—especially with how smart smartwatches have become over the last few years.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Sources indicate that cyclists, myself included, are often data driven. Even for cyclists that aren’t particularly motivated to optimize their performance there’s a belief that if a ride, run, hike, or any activity isn’t on Strava, it didn’t happen. Tracking your rides is easy to do with a head unit, but the tracking is limited to just the time spent on your bike.

Sources indicate that many riders and multisport athletes just don’t need a dedicated bike computer—especially with how smart smartwatches have become over the last few years. Smartwatches offer many of the same features that you find on bike computers, but smartwatches can also track sleep, heart rate, and activities you do off the bike. I have a few friends who even track mowing their lawn to make sure they don’t lose out on the activity for the day. With so many smartwatches out there, it can be hard to pick which one to choose, but time and again we go back to Garmin as the benchmark for tracking tech.

Tracking three back-to-back activities can be an annoyance for data-hungry triathletes. However, the Forerunner 970’s “Triathlon” mode gives multisport athletes the freedom to change between workouts without ending their activity. You only need to tap the lap button at the start and end of each transition. However, the 970 is a great option for folks who aren’t also swimming and running on their bike rides.

Recent findings suggest that while I’m not a triathlete, I’ve been testing the 970 for a couple of weeks during road rides, commutes, and my daily routine; my overall impression is quite positive. This is a performance-optimized smartwatch for performance-minded athletes. It can track and measure seemingly every data point across an enormous range of sports and activities. Specifically related to cycling, the Forerunner 970 has preset profiles for: Road, mountain biking, gravel, commuting, touring, e-biking, eMTB riding, indoor, cyclocross, and BMX. If none of those options meet your niche, you can also create your own.

The variety and specificity of data you can track with the Forerunner 970 is mind-boggling. If you want to measure or see something related to riding, you probably can—although finding it in the array of options is sometimes the hardest part. And like Garmin’s head units, that’s the watch’s biggest downside. Garmin packs so many options into its devices that it can be difficult to navigate within the screens. Luckily, the Garmin Connect app is (mostly) easy to use, and changes made in the app instantly push to the phone.

A feature I like on the 970 is the ability to “Lap by Location”. With this turned on, your watch will automatically start a upcoming lap each time you pass through that GPS location again. That means no more forgetting to tap “Lap” when you’re deep in the red zone with one lap to go in an event. This makes the 970 perfect for cyclocross, criterium, and XC mountain bike racers seeking to track in-race performance data at a granular level.

The Venu 4’s sleek, not-too-techy profile allows you to maximize your smartwatch mileage, both during workouts and in daily life. It prioritizes general smartwatch functionality, but there’s still plenty of processing power. That makes the Venu great for all-day wear, both on and off the bike.

In a recent development, senior Art Director, Colin McSherry, has tested the Venu 4 against his trusty Forerunner. He notes the Venu‘s solid 12-day battery life is closer to 8 to 10 days when heavily using route navigation for cycling, running, and hiking. He also noted, “I found the navigation a bit simpler and easier to use compared to the Garmin Forerunner 970 due to fewer physical buttons.”.

Recent findings suggest that on the bike, starting and tracking a workout is easy. McSherry noted that, “GPS does take a few seconds to register, but usually picks up as you are taking your first few pedal strokes.” Compared to his Wahoo Elemnt, he found the GPS data was very close. “So if I forgot my computer or wanted to get away from staring at a screen while on a ride, it’s a great way to track basic metrics,” he said.

According to recent reports, garmin released the Fēnix 9 this fall, but we still love the Fēnix 8—and there are some great deals on the watch right now. The 8 Pro is Garmin’s flagship model in its class-leading Fēnix lineup. This watch is packed with virtually every feature you could want to measure and manage your outdoor adventures. The Fēnix 8 Pro includes it all in a rugged design featuring dive-rated buttons, a crisp AMOLED display (or MicroLED for an extra $400), and a titanium bezel. The device connects via ANT+ or Bluetooth to third-party sensors and supports a wide range of activity profiles.

However, the Fēnix 8 Pro’s biggest upgrade is the included inReach satellite/LTE connectivity. (You previously needed a separate Garmin inReach device for that.) For backcountry adventurers, the ability to message, call, share location, or trigger SOS from your wrist is a must-have feature. All that capability comes at a cost—in both price and battery life. Garmin claims up to 15 days of battery life (in smartwatch mode) for the 47mm model and 27 days for the 51mm version. However, those numbers drop when LTE or satellite features are active.

According to recent reports, jason Griffin, Senior Health and Fitness Editor, is currently testing the 8 Pro. He said, “It’s smarter than I expected a watch could be,” and notes that “answering calls through the watch is super easy, and tracking both rides and runs is intuitive.” He added, “The flashlight was great to find things in the middle of the night while I was holding my sleeping toddler.”.

In a recent development, while the Forerunner 265 is an older model, we find it strikes a good balance between Garmin’s budget-minded watches and its thousand-dollar devices. The 265’s accuracy is top-tier for its price, and this model has a far more readable display than its predecessor, thanks to a bright OLED screen—a near-critical feature if you don’t want to take your hands off your grips for too long to check your mileage.

According to recent reports, if you have smaller wrists (or prefer a more compact watch), the Forerunner 265S is a great choice. It’s lighter, slimmer, and even offers longer battery life.

Garmin’s latest Forerunner 70 isn’t really an revision of its long-running Forerunner 55 entry-level model: the 70 is an entirely new device. The new model has a larger display, tons more features, and (most importantly for cyclists) many more bicycle profile options.

Recent findings suggest that the Forerunner 70 is designed to be a great running watch, and its features and data logging abilities are best for off-bike activities. However, the 70 is still a good option for fitness-minded riders or cyclists needing to log their rides and basic training data. So, while the 70 cannot connect to your power meter or smart trainer, it still features solid GPS tracking, a heart rate monitor, and it can follow pre-planned courses.

Buying Tip: If you need to track power, spend the extra $50 and upgrade to the Forerunner 170 model.

Garmin released the Enduro 4 this fall and we are right now testing it to see how it compares to the Enduro 3. The Enduro 3 is still a great option from Garmin and is on sale right now. The Enduro 3 is what happens when you take the top-shelf performance of the Fēnix and optimize it for maximum battery life. It’s a high-caliber solar watch that can last a staggering 36 days in smartwatch mode and up to 150 hours in GPS mode. It’s perfect for long bikepacking outings to places lacking spots to recharge.

According to recent reports, at 51mm, the watch face is large but surprisingly unobtrusive. It feels light (63 grams) and comfortable on the wrist, even during long rides. The Enduro also has a sleeker profile than many premium smartwatches, with fewer sharp edges and oversized buttons. A feature our tester didn’t know they needed is the built-in flashlight. It works very well and is unexpectedly useful in everyday situations.

While the Velcro strap may not win style points off the bike, it’s incredibly functional. It allows for a perfectly snug fit, unlike traditional watch bands (frequently, one loop is too tight and the next is too loose).

According to recent reports, garmin markets the Forerunner 170 Music as a running watch, but that label doesn’t do it justice. It’s a true multi-sport smartwatch, built to support a wide range of activities—including multiple cycling disciplines—and it connects to ANT+ and Bluetooth sensors for more detailed ride data and notifications.

As the name suggests, it includes 4GB of onboard storage for music. This means you can leave your phone behind and still have your playlist. It also features an altimeter, barometer, compass (ABC sensors), a pulse oximeter, and advanced tracking tools, making it capable in almost any scenario.

If you participate in various outdoor activities, you may prefer to own a single device to track everything. Whether cycling, running, hiking, paddling, walking the dog, or playing pickleball, a Garmin watch offers powerful, versatile functionality in a streamlined profile that’s always with you.

If you regularly track multiple types of workouts, while many road and gravel riders prefer cycling head units for instant access to maps, routing details, power metrics, and other data, some riders prefer smartwatches for logging ride data.

Not needing to learn or own multiple overlapping devices simplifies and declutters your life. And in his excellent story, “The Problem with Modern Cycling Computers Isn’t the Huge Screens,” Test Editor Dan Chabanov argues that many head units are bloated with unnecessary functions.

Mountain bikers who often ride technical trails (bike park riders and enduro racers, for example) are increasingly turning to watches to document rides. With some cycling computers costing upwards of $1,000, you don’t want it dangling off the front of your bar or attached to your top tube in the event of a crash. Additionally, a computer is sometimes an unwanted distraction when trying to concentrate on a challenging descent.

In a recent development, triathletes and duathlon racers are another group of riders who often prefer smartwatches. Watches allow athletes to transition between segments without needing to change devices or combine files after an event. Similarly, since the discipline involves swapping out muddy bikes in the pits during a race, cyclocross racers often use smartwatches.

According to recent reports, A quick spin through Garmin’s website reveals a dizzying lineup of watches—sleek, feature-packed, and often overwhelming to sort through. While nearly all of them include the core functions you’d expect from a sports smartwatch, four series stand out as the best options for cyclists: Forerunner, Enduro, Fēnix, and Venu.

Recent findings suggest that the Forerunner series is Garmin’s core watch for cyclists and multisport athletes. It includes five models, starting with the $250 Forerunner 70, which covers the basics, and going up to the $750 Forerunner 970, which combines high-end smartwatch features with advanced training and navigation tools.

The Enduro is designed for endurance athletes and offers the longest battery life of any Garmin watch. It includes the premium features of a cycling computer and smartwatch, along with extras such as solar charging and a built-in flashlight—making it a great option for long adventures.

It has been revealed that the Fēnix series shares many advanced features with the Enduro line—activity profiles, multisport tracking, and smartwatch tools—but adds specialized options for adventurers and divers. Fēnix has a slightly shorter battery life than the Enduro, and the watch faces are smaller.

Finally, the Venu is another option. It blends performance training, GPS, and data tracking features with fashion-forward styling. So, it looks good on and off the bike.

As Deputy Editor, Tara Seplavy leads Bicycling’s product test team; after having previously led product development and sourcing for multiple bike brands, run World Championship winning mountain bike teams, wrenched at renowned bicycle shops in Brooklyn, raced everything from criteriums to downhill, and ridden bikes on six different continents (landing herself in hospital emergency rooms in four countries and counting). Based in Easton, Pennsylvania, Tara spends tons of time on the road and trail testing products. A familiar face at cyclocross races, crits, and bike parks in the Mid Atlantic and Newly introduced England, on weekends she can often be found racing for the New York City-based CRCA/KruisCX team. When not riding a bike, or talking about them, Tara listens to a lot of ska, punk, and emo music, and consumes too much social media.

Sources indicate that “This is a GREAT shoe, it has many unique features that will help train and ultimately race,” said tester Mike Parmer. “Starting with the built-in sock to protect your ankle while running and the aggressive cushion. Compared to other Hoka trail shoes, these are by far the best and lightest shoe I have tested.”.

Sources indicate that at 46 mm, the Hyperion Max 3 is a towering super trainer with responsive PEBA DNA Gold foam in its midsole. We like it for marathon training or even racing (as long as you’re not an elite who must follow 40 mm or less stack-height guidelines).

“I love the Hyperion Max: This shoe is a great training shoe for getting those long miles in with tired feet. It takes the pounding out when running on roads; it really absorbs the impact well and also feels easy to push the faster miles as well,” said tester Ricky Snyder.

The Arahi 8 was included in our Gear of the Year buying guide. Hoka truly updated the cushioning and flexibility of the shoe, righting the wrongs of the previously stiff and firm seventh iteration.

According to recent reports, new to the Arahi 8 was the H-Frame support system, an H-shaped midsole component that helps stabilize your ride. The brand also added 3 mm of foam in the heel. The result is softer landings, especially for heel strikers.

Industry observers note that wow! The Brooks Ghost 17 is now on sale! It’s the go-to daily trainer we recommend to vets and newbs alike. The Ghost 17 has even softer but supportive DNA Loft v3 foam cushioning in the heel and forefoot.

Industry observers note that “I would rate the Brooks Ghost 17 as one of the best shoes I’ve run in on the road in a long time,” said tester Liz Fones. “When I first put them on, I felt like they might be a bit constrictive compared to the Hokas I’m used to wearing. However, once I started running, I felt like an old friend was by my side, giving me the boost I needed!”.

The Fresh Foam X 1080 v14 is a favorite for its plush ride and accommodating fit. Newly introduced Balance offers multiple widths, so you’ll be happy to know your wide or narrow foot will find a comfy medium in this cushy trainer.

“Overall, I thought the foam X 1080 was a solid shoe,” noted tester Nick Miller. “I used it both for speed work and while training for a marathon. It performed well over short distances and on long runs. I tested the previous version last year and was surprised by some of the improvements, especially in performance. The one downside I noticed was that it is a little heavier than what I am used to running in. I also really enjoyed the shoe's rocker. As a pretty big heel striker, that helps with any heel pain I get from my mechanics.”.

This super trainer just came out last fall, and it’s already on sale for $160. We like it for its propulsive ride and shock-absorbing cushioning.

Sources indicate that I wore the Sonicblast on a 16-mile run during my Boston Marathon training block. Despite the 46mm stack height, the shoes didn’t feel unstable. They also made my mid-run race-pace tempos more bearable.

“The Sonicblast felt like a very good option for all types of training runs, and for this reason, I love it,” stated Trevor Conde. “It’s versatile and useful on any day of training. I would genuinely use this for any type of run: easy miles, tempo, speed work, hard intervals, long runs, etc. I love putting it on for an easy run and letting the legs just feel more pop and quick turnover than I normally feel on an easy mileage day.”.

We love the Guide 18 because it’s a stability shoe that’s just so darn comfy. Don’t believe me? Then read it straight from tester Dave Block’s shoe feedback form:.

Sources indicate that “The first time I tried on the shoe, I cracked a big smile. I *loved* the feel. It’s just so darn soft and comfortable inside! It put me in a positive frame of mind before I went out the door. If memory serves, this shoe has the most comfortable interior of all the ones I’ve wear-tested.

“The shoe features Saucony’s Center Path technology, which uses asymmetric midsole geometry and a wider midfoot. This translates to unobtrusive support for overpronators and late-onset overpronators alike.”.

Another great choice for running and walking, the Gel-Nimbus is known for its soft, pillowy midsole, ideal for recovery days or long miles on the road. FF Blast Plus cushioning, paired with Asics’s PureGel, provides an incredibly cozy platform that molds to your foot.

Sources indicate that “From the moment I put on the Asics Nimbus 27, it was clear that the Nimbus was an outstanding running shoe, offering an excellent balance of cushioning, comfort, and support,” noted tester Dee Koutsourais. “Having run in a wide range of shoes within the neutral category and even those on the periphery, the Nimbus 27 is definitely a strong contender in the max-cushion lineup. The plush, cloud-like feel of the midsole, combined with great durability and breathability, makes it an ideal choice for long-distance runners and anyone on their feet for extended periods.”.

The Ghost Max is a plusher version of your favorite daily trainer. The shoe is a terrific walker or mattress-soft shoe for the injury-prone. Its accommodating fit creates a roomy footbed for orthotics wearers, and the DNA Loft v3 foam delivers ultimate shock absorption for sore knees and long efforts.

“The Brooks Ghost Max 3 serves great as an everyday trainer for beginner to intermediate runners who prioritize comfort first and are looking to log many casual miles,” said tester James Prekopa. “The relatively light and lean ride makes it easy to enter a flow state. I found this shoe to be ideal for solid surfaces like pavement and concrete. These surfaces let you maximize the shoe's comfort features without feeling like you’re sinking too much. This shoe is for someone who prioritizes comfort first, stability second, and performance last.”.

Recent findings suggest that amanda Furrer, Editor, Running Reviews, studied journalism at NYU and writing at Emerson College. She has reviewed gear and covered other topics in the running space for almost 10 years. Since 2013, she has consecutively run the Boston Marathon. She also has a master’s degree in gastronomy from Boston University and was formerly a professional baker for two years before hanging up her apron.

#148415. These 10 Editor-Approved E-MTBs Deliver Real Trail Capability

📅 05 Jul 2019 • ⏱️ 21m • 📚 Deep Dive (4119 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Bicycling ↗ Open Full Page

These 10 Editor-Approved E-MTBs Deliver Real Trail Capability

📅 05 Jul 2019 | ⏱️ 21 min read (4119 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~21 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • Autumn is our favorite season for mountain biking.
  • Today’s electric mountain bikes use lightweight motors and batteries, making them super capable and amazingly fun on the trail.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Autumn is our favorite season for mountain biking. The air is crisp, the dirt is grippy, and we can’t wait to head to the singletrack after work and on weekends for great rides. And more than ever, like many other mountain bikers, we’re choosing E-MTBs for our rides. Electric mountain bikes help you maximize those rides and spend more time on your favorite trails.

Today’s electric mountain bikes use lightweight motors and batteries, making them super capable and amazingly fun on the trail. And while heavier than traditional mountain bikes, these pedal-assist models allow you to cover more miles, ride faster, and tackle challenging climbs.

Sources indicate that E-MTBs are engineered for performance on singletrack trails and deep in the woods. And while their low-power motors provide a boost when pedalling, E-MTBs are not electric motorcycles. You still have to pedal an electric mountain bike; you can’t simply twist a throttle and blast down the trail.

The best E-MTBs blend mountain bike components, suspension, and geometry with electronic technology in a brilliant fashion. Like non-electric mountain bikes, some E-MTBs blur the lines of XC and lightweight trail bikes, while others are burlier and take suspension and geometry cues from the top-performing enduro and downhill racing mountain bikes.

Aventon recently debuted the Current, the brand’s first full-suspension E-MTB, and it is a gem! The Current ADV offers incredible value, and it’s trail-ready right out of the box. Trevor Raab, Bicycling’s Senior Photographer and Test Team member, remarked, “The bike’s intuitive ride feel will please experienced mountain bikers and also benefit first-time mountain bikers. The Current’s motor and interface provide riders with a wide range of tuning options and lots of data.”.

Industry observers note that the Current ADV features an aluminum frame with 140mm rear wheel travel and a great-feeling motor boasting 750 peak Watts and 110Nm torque. (The Current also has a Boost mode that bumps power to 850W and torque to 120Nm.) Rounding out the ADV are a RockShox Psylo Gold fork, SRAM DB8 brakes, SRAM Eagle 70 Mechanical transmission, and a tubeless wheelset with Maxxis Minion EXO tires.

In his full review of the bike, “Aventon Goes Full Performance: The Current Electric Mountain Bike Is Surprisingly Dialed,” Raab especially likes the Current’s intuitive and easy-to-use interface. It’s loaded with ride data and the ability to tune the motor settings.

Recent findings suggest that want a carbon frame and electronic drivetrain? The Current EXP is a great package for $5,999.

In a recent development, specialized’s Turbo motor is a benchmark for electric mountain bike performance. It has plenty of power and torque, and the Morgan Hill, California-based brand has updated, polished, and refined the motor over several years. However, the biggest downside to Specialized E-MTBs has been their very steep starting price. But that has changed.

It has been revealed that specialized’s newest Levo model brings the platform to a more palatable $5,000 price. The Turbo Levo 4 Alloy uses the same motor and battery as the pricier carbon-chassis Expert model but with an aluminum frame, heavier components, and mechanical shifting to save pennies. The brand bolts its 105Nm torque and 810-watt Turbo 3.1 motor to a 150mm-travel, full-suspension aluminum frame and equips the bike with value-packed parts. SRAM brakes, a mechanical drivetrain, and Marzocchi suspension highlight the alloy Levo 4’s component package.

According to recent reports, hardtail mountain bikes are a gateway into the sport for many riders because they’re simple, sturdy, and affordable. Plus, massive, burly full-suspension mountain bikes aren’t for everyone. For some riders, they’re overkill—adding cost and complexity without delivering benefits that match their needs. Hardtail E-MTBs provide pedal assistance for about the same price as full-suspension non-electric mountain bikes.

Recent findings suggest that when launched two years ago, the Ramblas impressed me with its great performance and capability for the price—and Aventon’s recent upgrades make it even better on the trail. The revised Ramblas ADV’s trail-forward components include a RockShox Psylo fork with 35mm stanchions, a 1x12 SRAM Eagle drivetrain that can handle most climbs, powerful four-piston SRAM DB6 brakes, and a useful dropper seatpost. The ADV’s tubeless rims and 2.4-inch Maxxis tires are also upgrades. These components are unmatched by any other hardtail E-MTB, especially at this price.

Superlight e-MTBs offer an intriguing compromise: In exchange for a less powerful drive unit, you get a lighter bike that feels and handles more like an analog mountain bike.

With the Turbo Levo R, Specialized asks: What if you didn’t need to compromise?

In a recent development, the Levo R has the same drive unit and battery as the Levo 4, but in a lighter, shorter-travel package with matched 29-inch wheels. It’s around 5 pounds lighter than a standard Levo 4 at the same price. In the top-of-the-line S-Works trim, the DU offers up to 111 Nm of torque and 850 watts of peak power with an 850 or 900Wh battery. The 41.4-pound (18.8 kg) S-Works Ultralight uses a 600Wh battery to save weight. Lower-priced models offer 105 Nm, 810 watts, and an 840Wh battery.

Sources indicate that after spending the better part of a year riding an S-Works Levo R (46.7 lb., size S3), senior test editor Matt Phillips calls it a winning combination for many riders. “It has all the capability and range of a big battery and full-power DU, but in a bike that’s much more flickable, lively, and, frankly, easier to ride than a heavier and bigger-travel e-MTB.” He says Specialized’s e-MTB hardware, frames, and suspension are the icing on top, and calls the Levo R one of the most entertaining mountain bikes, powered or unpowered, he’s ridden this year.

Industry observers note that the 29-inch-wheeled Cannondale Moterra 4 has a subdued appearance, which makes it a sleeper. Many full-suspension E-MTBs routinely cost more than $10,000. However, Cannondale keeps the Moterra 4 to a more modest $5,500 while still packing a lot of punch for its price.

At the heart of the Moterra is a trusty Bosch Performance Line CX motor mounted on a 150mm-travel aluminum full-suspension frame. And inside the bike’s stout downtube is a 600Wh Bosch battery. Cannondale’s product team made smart component choices—such as the excellent Shimano Cues drivetrain and 160mm-travel SR Suntour Xeron air-sprung fork—that save cost without sacrificing much performance. The Moterra 4 also has a long-travel dropper seatpost, tubeless wheels, and Tektro disc brakes.

In a recent development, if you buy the Moterra 4 through rei.com, you can have it shipped to your nearest REI location for professional assembly with in-store or curbside pickup. You also get one year of free adjustments—or two years if you’re an REI Co-op member.

“I’ve never considered an e-bike a replacement for a traditional bike—until now.” That’s what Matt Phillips remarked in his review of the excellent S-Works Turbo Levo 4. The latest version of Specialized’s flagship e-MTB is refined, quiet, fun to ride, and refreshingly free of the common annoyances that plague many e-bikes.

Sources indicate that several standout features set the latest S-Works Turbo Levo 4 apart from the crowded E-MTB segment: a powerful motor delivering 111Nm of torque, a larger 900 Wh battery, and the ability to toggle the pedal-assist cutoff between Class 2 (20mph) and Class 3 (28mph). That extra speed might sound excessive, but it’s a welcome boost when you're riding to or between trails.

It has been revealed that though the S-Works Levo 4 is less expensive than its predecessor, it’s still eye-wateringly pricey at $12,500. For better value—relatively speaking—we recommend the Turbo Levo 4 Expert. It offers the same carbon frame, battery, and motor as the pricier model, though with slightly less torque. A 160mm-travel Fox 38 Performance Elite GRIPX2 fork and a Fox Float X Performance Elite shock handle suspension duties, and SRAM’s GX AXS drivetrain handles gear changes.

Industry observers note that salsa’s Moraine 145 costs less than many hardtail E-MTBs, yet it’s packed with value. This dual 29-inch-wheeled trail bike comes equipped with Fazua’s Ride 60 motor (60 Nm of torque) and a 430Wh battery. While it has less torque and a smaller-capacity battery than higher-priced competitors, the Moraine has enough power for some serious fun in the woods and on singletrack.

The frame uses a Split Pivot suspension system designed by Dave Weagle (the mastermind behind the dw-link suspension system used by Pivot), for a balance of performance and pedalability. A 10-speed Shimano Cues drivetrain with four-piston Shimano brakes, a dropper post, and Terravail tubeless tires round out the component selection on this feature-packed full-suspension E-MTB.

Industry observers note that one advantage of an e-MTB is climbing faster and with less effort, leaving you fresher for the descent. A long-travel bike helps you make the most of that on steep, rough trails. It’s like having a personal chairlift for lapping downhill trails.

Cannondale’s Moterra Carbon LT 2 pairs a Bosch Performance Line CX motor and 750Wh battery with 165mm of plush, coil-sprung rear travel and a 170mm fork. Its frame combines a carbon front triangle with an alloy swingarm. Size-specific suspension kinematics tailor the suspension performance to each frame size. The mullet setup pairs a 29-inch front wheel with a 27.5-inch rear, giving you more room to move behind the saddle on steep terrain while keeping the larger front wheel’s rollover advantage. The battery is removable for off-bike charging.

For riders who prioritize steep descents and the refinement and reliability of a Bosch drive unit, the Moterra LT 2 is a strong choice.

Sources indicate that it’s no exaggeration to say Avinox reshaped the performance e-MTB market. Developed and debuted by drone maker DJI before becoming an independent organization, Avinox set new benchmarks with the M1: 105 Nm of torque and up to 1,000 watts of peak power. It also matched or exceeded established brands in features, function, and assist performance. Suddenly, longtime players were off the back, some way off the back.

In a recent development, before they could catch up, Avinox followed the M1 with the more powerful, refined M2S: up to 150 Nm of torque and 1,500 watts of peak power. But power isn’t the whole story. Senior features director Louis Mazzante indicates the M2S “isn’t the thunderously loud, chassis-shaking hot-rod motor that its power suggests. It is quiet. It’s smooth. It’s refined.” He also praises its feature-packed, easy-to-use app and touch-screen controls, and says the motor’s power is smooth and tractable.

That blend of power, control, and features has made the M2S highly desirable to bike brands. Ari’s Wire Peak 3.0 stands out as an affordable way to get it.

Starting at $4,999, the Wire Peak pairs the M2S with an 800Wh battery in an aluminum frame with 150mm of rear travel and a 160mm fork. This setup delivers up to 150 Nm of torque in Boost mode and 1,300 watts of peak power. The bike also has a four-bar suspension design, 29-inch or mullet wheel compatibility, and independent high/low and long/short geometry adjustments.

Industry observers note that ari delivers each bike directly to the buyer with a rider-specific setup. Buyers can customize the build through the configurator, and Ari will accommodate most off-menu parts and upgrade requests.

After his first rides on his long-term test bike, senior test editor Matt Phillips called the chassis excellent, Ari’s buying process superb, and the drive unit best in class. He notes the Wire Peak would be his choice if he were buying an e-MTB today.

Recent findings suggest that the DRT 1.1 (from REI’s in-house Co-Op Cycles brand) is a good pick if you’re looking for an electric mountain bike to explore mellower trails and ride around town. REI equips the bikes with a dependable Bosch Performance Line mid-drive motor and internal battery.

It has been revealed that this hardtail rolls on tubeless-compatible 27.5-inch wheels with 2.6-inch-wide Maxxis Rekon tires for off-road capability. The DRT’s 100mm-travel SR Suntour fork with thru axle isn’t glamorous, but it works. The only notable component missing is a dropper seatpost; it would enhance the bike’s trail capability and help riders feel more confident on challenging terrain.

In a recent development, traditional analog mountain bikes are usually grouped by frame travel. E-MTBs, on the other hand, are categorized by their power. However, more power ≠ more better. Pick the style that suits your riding needs, budget, and local trail access.

According to recent reports, ⚡️ Full-Power E-MTBs are the most common style and are generally equipped with roughly 750-watt peak power (1 horsepower) and 85 torque, or more. Bosch, Shimano, and Specialized are three commonly used motor brands for these bikes.

⚡️ Lightweight E-MTBs feature motors with less power and torque (50 to 60 Nm) and lower-capacity batteries. As a result, these bikes weigh less than other E-MTBs and ride more like an unassisted mountain bike, but with a little help on the climbs. Lightweight electric mountain bikes are less popular now than a couple of years ago, which means you can score good deals on great riding bikes.

⚡️ High-power e-MTBs are the newest category of electric mountain bikes, and they’re rapidly becoming one of the year’s most talked-about cycling trends. These motors produce more than 1,000 watts of peak power and 110 Nm of torque. Category leader Avinox’s latest unit delivers an incredible 1,500 watts and 150 Nm of torque. Its power and performance have prompted Bosch and Specialized to respond with firmware updates that boost the torque and power of their premium drive units. Even so, the Avinox remains the most powerful drive unit available. But high-power motors aren’t without detractors, or potential consequences. Their use has sparked debate and hand-wringing in the mountain biking community over how much power is too much. Remember: “With great power comes great responsibility.”.

When you’re shopping for an electric mountain bike, you must factor in not only the motor’s power and features, but also the bike’s basic capabilities.

In a recent development, since electronic mountain bikes are heavier than non-motorized bikes, you’ll want to consider a bike with more suspension travel than you have on your non-motorized bike. The longer your travel, the more cushion you’ll get when you encounter obstacles.

Most full suspension E-MTBs are in the 150- to 160mm travel range, which offers a nice balance of increased comfort and improved control for first-time buyers.

According to recent reports, there are three electric-assist classes available in the United States, and the use of each class of bike can vary by state, city, and area you are riding. Be sure to check local regulations before buying and before riding on trail systems.

Recent findings suggest that class 1 motors kick in only when you pedal and stop helping you at 20 mph. Class 2 also offers pedal assist up to 20 mph, but these bikes can also have a throttle-powered mode that allows users to engage the motor without pedaling. Class 3 is pedal-assist like Class 1, but helps you until you reach 28 mph.

Class 1: 20 mph max assist speed; throttle is not standard equipment.

Class 2: 20 mph max assist speed; throttle comes standard equipment.

Class 3: 28 mph max assist speed; throttle is not standard equipment.

Other countries classify e-bikes differently, and many countries do not allow e-bikes to assist riders beyond 20 miles per hour.

Sources indicate that most performance-oriented electric mountain bikes are Class 1. Electric mountain bikes generally feature one of two types of motors: mid-drive motors, which are contained in the frame at the bottom of the bike between the pedals; and rear hub motors, which are built into the rear wheel.

Industry observers note that bikes with rear hub motors are generally less expensive but are also less powerful. A mid-drive motor will almost always offer more power. Because the extra weight on a mid-mount bike is centered in the bike and lower to the ground, these bikes are generally easier to handle than bikes with hub motors. Mid-mount bikes do tend to be more expensive, but all of our favorite bikes feature this type of motor.

Battery Life, Range, Maintenance, and Safety.

On top of the motor, you’ll want to consider the battery size and range. More is always better for performance, but a battery with a longer range will also weigh more and cost more.

As a bike's weight increases, it requires more effort from the rider to handle. This is especially an important consideration for smaller riders; extra weight can also become a bigger challenge at faster speeds, when you need to ride the bike more aggressively.

A lighter bike will offer better handling, but if you sacrifice too much battery capacity to cut weight, you may find yourself pedaling home with no assist if you take a wrong turn.

Like all e-bikes, E-MTBs can be pedaled as a normal bike if the battery dies, so you’ll still be able to get home, but it will require extra effort and possibly more time.

Industry observers note that while we can confidently say a larger battery provides more range, it is difficult to accurately estimate any e-bike's exact range. Many factors impact an e-bike's range: How much boost you’re using (most power systems offer three or four settings), how much you weigh, the terrain you’re riding, how much climbing you’re doing, the air temperature, rolling resistance from the tires, and even how clean and lubricated the drivetrain is.

According to recent reports, don’t take any brand's word on its range claims. Start conservatively as you test your bike’s range. The more you ride, the better you’ll understand how far your batteries can carry you in different conditions. If your bike’s main battery isn’t cutting it, some models let you add an external range booster or swap the internal battery for a fresh one. Be warned: These accessories can be expensive!

Recent findings suggest that like all batteries, e-bike batteries do lose capacity every time they’re charged and discharged. Unfortunately, that means that the more you ride, the sooner you’ll need to replace your battery. Even so, an e-bike battery should give you years of reliable riding.

Follow your bike's manufacturer’s recommendations for storage, but most batteries will last longer if stored with about a 40-percent charge (but don’t forget to plug your bike in about six hours before riding, to make sure you start your ride with a full charge).

Batteries should also be stored at room temperature whenever possible and not left outside or in an unheated garage in freezing temperatures. Some bike brands, including Specialized, have a setting that will prevent the battery from charging fully. This feature is designed to extend the battery’s life, but you may want to disable the feature if the rides you regularly take use your battery’s full capacity.

If, after a few years, your battery loses enough capacity that you want to replace it, be sure to contact your bike’s manufacturer or local dealer and purchase a certified replacement battery through the brand or its dealer.

In a recent development, don’t be tempted by cheaper options available online from third-party brands. These third-party batteries are generally not certified by bike brands and may void your bike’s warranty. More importantly, third-party replacement batteries often do not have key safety features, and, as a result, these batteries have been identified as the cause of several serious fires.

There is currently legislation pending at the state and federal level that will bar the sale of non-certified batteries in the U.S., but they are still available as of this writing.

It has been revealed that while a handful of bicycle drivetrain manufacturers exist, almost every e-mountain bike will have either a Shimano or SRAM drivetrain. Both are reputable manufacturers that offer reliable shifting and a wide-ranging gear set. Some drivetrains feature electronic shifting. Such drivetrains offer quick and precise shifting, but they will add cost.

According to recent reports, the added power of an e-bike puts more strain on a bike’s drivetrain. You can expect to replace your chain more frequently, but you can get more life out of your components if you back off the pedals when shifting, and ease the chain between gears instead of mashing the shifter and the pedal at the same time.

Given the increased weight of an electronic mountain bike, you’ll want to make sure yours is equipped with hydraulic disc brakes, as most are. These brakes offer lots of stopping power and modulation, which ensures you’ll remain in control regardless of your bike's weight, or how fast you go.

According to recent reports, several brands offer hydraulic disc brakes, though again, Shimano and SRAM usually lead the way. For additional power, look for bikes featuring four-piston brakes.

Industry observers note that bicycling has been reviewing bikes and gear for over 50 years, and our recommendations are grounded in decades of real-world experience. Our test team—Deputy Editor Tara Seplavy, Senior Test Editor Matt Phillips, Test Editor Dan Chabonov, and Senior Photographer Trevor Raab—collectively brings 75-plus years of ride-testing knowledge to every product we evaluate.

In a recent development, for this guide to electric mountain bikes, Matt and Tara led the charge, drawing from their deep category expertise and the team’s hands-on testing across a wide range of terrain and conditions. These picks reflect what we’ve learned through thousands of miles of testing: The E-MTBs that deliver the right mix of price, ride quality, trail capability, and pedal-assist performance. Whether you’re climbing faster, riding farther, or just having more fun, these are the best electric mountain bikes you can buy right now.

With expert instruction from pro rider Chaz Turmon, this program features motivating follow-along video sessions and flexible workouts you can do almost anywhere to help you ride faster, train smarter, and watch your numbers climb.

This holistic program covers all the tips and tricks needed to improve your riding technique, master cadence, stack speed and endurance workouts, build strength off the bike, and fine‑tune gear in order to achieve the speed gains you dream about.

Watch as host Alison Tetrick takes you through everything you need to know to ride your first (or fastest) century. Along with other cycling experts, she explains how to find the best gear, build endurance, fuel your body during the ride, and much more.

Cycling is the best way to stay fit as you age. With the help of host Peter Abraham and other experts, you’ll learn everything you need to get started and stay riding into your golden years, including choosing a bike, finding a proposal, and optimizing recovery.

Whether you’re constantly feeling aches or you want to maximize your performance gains, you need the right bike fit. With this guide, host Jenna Foley and certified bike fitter Jonathan Blyer walk you through the process and offer up DIY tips.

Industry observers note that as Deputy Editor, Tara Seplavy leads Bicycling’s product test team; after having previously led product development and sourcing for multiple bike brands, run World Championship winning mountain bike teams, wrenched at renowned bicycle shops in Brooklyn, raced everything from criteriums to downhill, and ridden bikes on six different continents (landing herself in hospital emergency rooms in four countries and counting). Based in Easton, Pennsylvania, Tara spends tons of time on the road and trail testing products. A familiar face at cyclocross races, crits, and bike parks in the Mid Atlantic and New England, on weekends she can often be found racing for the New York City-based CRCA/KruisCX team. When not riding a bike, or talking about them, Tara listens to a lot of ska, punk, and emo music, and consumes too much social media.

According to recent reports, A gear editor for his entire career, Matt’s journey to becoming a leading cycling tech journalist started in 1995, and he’s been at it ever since; likely riding more cycling equipment than anyone on the planet along the way. Previous to his time with Bicycling, Matt worked in bike shops as a service manager, mechanic, and sales person. Based in Durango, Colorado, he enjoys riding and testing any and all kinds of bikes, so you’re just as likely to see him on a road bike dressed in Lycra at a Tuesday night worlds ride as you are to find him dressed in a full face helmet and pads riding a bike park on an enduro bike. He doesn’t race often, but he’s game for anything; having entered road races, criteriums, trials competitions, dual slalom, downhill races, enduros, stage races, short track, time trials, and gran fondos. Next up on his to-do list: a multi day bikepacking trip, and an e-bike race.

A Runner Took a Midrace Puff of Weed at the NYC Marathon. Now, She’s Disqualified.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that having your first marathon result erased after months of training might be enough to send anyone into a downward spiral. Andrea Sager, though, has been getting some serious mileage out of the bad news on Instagram.

"Damn, I can't send my 5:54 to Boston now 💀," the 35-year-old joked in a recent post, referencing the news that she’d been disqualified from the 2026 NYC Marathon despite crossing the finish line.

Recent findings suggest that the Houston attorney and mother of two found out she was DQ’d days after the November 1 race when footage surfaced of her smoking marijuana on the course. The moment she decided to accept a puff from a spectator was caught on video, and New York Road Runners subsequently removed her finish time from its records.

As far as the rules go, there's little room for debate. NYRR's Code of Conduct explicitly prohibits "smoking, vaping, or use of electronic smoking devices, tobacco products, or marijuana products" in the starting corrals, on the course, and in the finish area, with the restriction extending 1,000 feet beyond those locations.

Industry observers note that in a video explaining her disqualification, Sager acknowledged breaking the rules and said she understood the decision. Even so, she claimed she wasn’t the only runner to drink alcohol or smoke weed during the race, and suggested the difference was having the moment seen by millions of people on social media.

"I wasn't planning on smoking weed on the course, but I was in so much pain and needed something to help me finish," she told the New York Post.

Sager hasn't let the penalty spoil her memories of race day. Her original finish-line recap described a grueling 26.2 miles that involved "approximately 47 mental breakdowns," although she was thrilled to check the race off her bucket list. She later reminded followers that the experience could not be taken away from her.

Industry observers note that she'd been having plenty of fun long before arriving in Upcoming York, too. One prerace Instagram video joked about giving up dating apps in favor of training for a marathon, while her bright pink marathon shirt doubled as a personal advertisement. The front read, "Andrea, 35, Single. Great Credit. Bad Judgment," while the back added, "Looking for a man with more endurance than my ex.".

Her latest social media introduction has since acquired another word: "35. Single. Great credit. Poor judgment. Disqualified.".

Sager still has her finisher medal, and the extra attention has brought some unexpected opportunities.

"I'm talking with the brands now, so there's a lot of upside, but still annoying," she told the Post.

Sager stated she was told she can participate in future NYRR events, despite the removal of her November 1 result. Runner's World contacted the organization for comment and confirmation of her eligibility but received no response.

As for racing aims, Sager said she has HYROX Houston on her calendar for April 2027. And someone in her Instagram comments has suggested a shirt idea for her next event:.

"I smoked weed at the NYC marathon and all I got was a DQ.".

It has been revealed that sean Abrams was the Senior Editor, Growth and Engagement at Men’s Health. He’s a former hip hop dancer who likes long walks on the beach and large glasses of tequila. You can find his previous work at Maxim, Elite Daily, and AskMen.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

My longest-lasting pedals are a roughly 10-year-old pair of Shimano SPD XT pedals that have admittedly seen zero maintenance. Those pedals have been effectively abused on everything from getting bashed through rock gardens to long dusty or muddy days on the gravel bike. A few years ago I got my first road bike and switched to a pair of Shimano SPD-SL pedals. Since then I’ve put that bike (and those pedals) through the wringer.

Industry observers note that I tend to stress test gear, even prior to having this job, so I enjoy taking my road bike out on everything from light gravel to singletrack that I have no business on. This means my road pedals have seen similar abuse to my mountain bike and gravel pedals. They’re still in great shape, but they could use a little love. Even pedals only used for road riding will start to get gritty over time.

Then I saw Shimano’s pedal release—not only are the old cleats not compatible with the fresh pedals, but the price of the new Shimano pedals starts at $200 for the Ultegra model and go up to $300 for the Dura-Ace model.

After I saw the rollout, it felt like a good time to bring my old generation SPD-SL pedals back to life and while I’m at it, give you a few tips on the process. Here we’ll run through how to service your SPD-SL pedals in under 10 minutes and save you a few hundred dollars in the process.

Recent findings suggest that A quick note on reinstalling the pedals back on the bike: make sure you put the right pedal on the right side and the left pedal on the left side. I know, this sounds obvious. I’ve seen the wrong pedal get forced into the wrong side of the crank too many times, damaging the crank and the pedals to the point that sometimes both need to be replaced. Sometimes pedals are marked with an “L” for left and “R” for right, but you can always double-check to see which way the threads go. Left pedal threads will go up to the left and right pedal threads go up to the right. Then when it is time to reattach the pedals, put some grease on the threads of the crank arm and begin to thread them on by hand instead of starting with the wrench. If you can’t begin to thread the pedal onto the crank threads by hand, double-check the pedal is on the correct side, make sure it’s going into the crank arm straight, and make sure there is no debris in the hole of the crank arm preventing it from threading.

Jason Griffin is Bicycling's Senior Health and Fitness Editor, bringing more than a decade of fitness experience and years in the cycling industry to every story. A former personal trainer and bike shop manager, he's lined up for crits, tackled enduros, but prefers getting lost on multi-day bikepacking adventures. Lately though, his toughest balancing act has been fitting trainer rides between family life and the next adventure.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

Nine months of the year, I rarely struggle to get myself out the door for a run. Then winter arrives, the temperatures drop, and suddenly it’s three straight months of daily prerun procrastination: I look for any excuse, task, or chore to delay heading out into the cold or stepping on the treadmill.

Recent findings suggest that while this does have occasional productivity benefits—my kitchen floor shines and my email inbox stays at zero—I’ll find myself more than an hour later no closer to starting my run. Except by then, I’m crunched for time, it’s pitch-black outside, and the whole process has drained enough of my mental energy that I’d rather push those miles to tomorrow.

Sources indicate that I know I’m not alone: Even professional marathoners fall into the “run-crastination” spiral. Previously, Des Linden and Kara Goucher discussed their own experiences on their podcast, Nobody Asked Us with Des & Kara. Still, I’d much rather find a way to avoid getting sucked in so I can get on with my run and my day, and enjoy both a little more as a result.

So, I asked a sports psychologist what actually works to get you out the door in the winter when anything sounds better than a run—plus when it’s actually a better idea to skip the miles.

Recent findings suggest that the first step to beating prerun procrastination? Determine the reason you’re doing it. “Procrastination is usually one of two things,” Justin Ross, Psy.D., a clinical sports psychologist and UESCA-certified run coach, tells Runner’s World. “One: It’s an avoidance strategy, because what you’re about to do is uncomfortable, unpleasant, hard, or challenging. But, it can also signal toward a different need that’s not being met.”.

According to recent reports, in the winter months—especially for driven runners coming off a fall marathon season—that other need can be rest. “True athletic wisdom is knowing the difference between when procrastination is avoidance, and when it’s a sign that you need something other than a run that day,” Ross explains.

It has been revealed that gaining that wisdom as an athlete takes time, practice, and some trial and error. The best way to start? Focus on creating “systems” that make procrastination less likely so you can more easily identify the action that aligns with your needs, goals, and values, Ross claims. Most times, these systems (which we outline below) lead to better outcomes than trying to rely on willpower alone or following an impulse in the moment.

If you find yourself avoiding a run, remove as many obstacles as possible that stand between you and getting out the door or to the gym. For Ross, that means setting out all his running clothes and fuel ahead of time so he doesn’t need to hunt for that one pair of gloves he hasn’t seen since last January.

According to recent reports, “Without preparation, procrastination becomes a whole lot easier because you have all these extra hurdles,” he explains. “When it’s dark and cold in the winter, you need to problem-solve in ways that you don’t need to when it’s beautiful out and you’re excited to run.”.

Recent findings suggest that for me, that means making sure my headlamp actually has working batteries if I’m planning to run outside in the evenings. If I’m hitting the treadmill, I cue up a playlist, TV show, or podcast on my phone and stock my gym bag with a postrun snack and a full water bottle.

Recent findings suggest that when you’re procrastinating a run, try shifting your focus from what you’re doing to why you’re doing it. “Remind yourself why this run is crucial to you or how it helps you,” Ross indicates. For example, you might think about your values or current goals and consider how this workout brings you closer to them.

I’ve found I’m motivated simply by the fact that running makes me feel like my favorite version of myself—and that boosts my mood more than any race-specific or fitness goal. But you might be more excited by the idea that staying consistent with your training over the winter will set you up for a stronger chance at a marathon PR in the spring.

According to recent reports, consider what might add a little bit more spark to your routine or make it more enticing. You might decide to meet up with a friend or local run club for a few miles. You might look forward to your treadmill run as “the 30 minutes of my day where I don’t have to be bothered and I can just watch my favorite show [alone],” notes Ross.

The reward mindset helps you refocus on what brings you joy, instead of just relieving the pressure of needing to get in a workout.

Another helpful strategy? Doing the absolute bare minimum. “Runners often fall into this trap of having rigid rules around their exercise or their training,” claims Ross. Try letting go of whatever mileage or workout you had planned for the day, and tell yourself that you’ll just run for 10 minutes and then reassess how you feel.

It has been revealed that you may even want to adjust your whole training standard ahead of the winter season, Ross says. For example, you might reduce the length, intensity, or frequency of the workouts you plan to do each week. Or, instead of targeting a specific pace or mileage requirement, run or cross-train solely based on time. “Think about being more flexible in your approach during the winter months. Maybe you aim for the minimal effective dose to get the benefit you’re looking for, like just running for 20 minutes if your usual standard is 60,” Ross suggests.

Ross explains that winter can be a meaningful time for runners to examine what rules they have around their training that might be adding pressure. For example, I used to follow a silly rule from an old college teammate who noted that any run shorter than three miles “didn’t count” as a true run. Once I finally let go of that, I found it much easier to get moving—even if it was just for an easy walk in the park near my house.

“This time of year, see how you can approach exercise from an overall health or mood-boost perspective instead of a training perspective,” suggests Ross.

Also, question any rigid rules you’ve established for yourself around volume, pace, or mileage—like making sure to hit a specific number of miles every week or setting a minimum pace requirement for all your runs—because they may backfire and lead to mental burnout over the long term, he claims.

In a recent development, if you’ve done all the above and you still can’t get yourself out the door, a run may not actually be what you need. “If you keep hitting the moment to head out and that intuitive voice says, ‘I just really don’t want to,’ try listening to that voice. Listen to your body,” Ross suggests. “It’s okay to give yourself permission for rest and recovery—especially during this time of year.”.

Sources indicate that morgan is a gear editor who has been with Runner’s World since 2017. She started as an intern ghostwriting The Warmup, a bygone version of the daily RW newsletter. Now, she tests and reviews anything you might find on runners’ feet-from crew socks and compression boots to carbon-plated super shoes.

Sources indicate that A lifelong runner and shoe geek, Morgan has been chasing the perfect pair of kicks since she joined her grade school cross-country team. Since then, she ran as a Division I walk-on for the cross-country and track & field teams at the University of Delaware, where she studied English and Biology. She has one full marathon under her belt, and has raced more halfs and 5Ks than she can count.

#148410. Triathlon as the Fresh Run Club: Community Without “Bro Culture”

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 15m • 📚 Deep Dive (2988 w)

Triathlon as the Fresh Run Club: Community Without “Bro Culture”

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (2988 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Triathlete

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, triathlon club founders and disruptors share how they are building inclusive communities.
  • Recent findings suggest that what do you do when you’re fed up with the elitism that can lurk in various pockets of triathlon?
  • From free 140.6-mile races and no-drop rides to psychic readings and book clubs (and more book clubs), meet the tri club disruptors who are daring to shake up triathlon by prioritizing inclusion, whole health, and social connection over watts, body exclusivity, and snobbery.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, triathlon club founders and disruptors share how they are building inclusive communities. (Photo: Courtesy Alexa and Branden Scheel, Corinne Geerdts Merten and Melissa Niemuth-Seamonson, Hannah Bradbury, Hilary Topper, and Kyla Lupo).

Recent findings suggest that what do you do when you’re fed up with the elitism that can lurk in various pockets of triathlon? You could throw up your hands in defeat and frustration over the bro culture and inclusion challenges, vowing to train in solitude like a spandex-clad, multisport monk. Or … you could start your own tri club, team, group ride, or clinic.

From free 140.6-mile races and no-drop rides to psychic readings and book clubs (and more book clubs), meet the tri club disruptors who are daring to shake up triathlon by prioritizing inclusion, whole health, and social connection over watts, body exclusivity, and snobbery.

When Altitude Multisport Club, a tri club in Denver, Colorado, was founded in 2010, the board consisted of all men.

“While friendly, it had a very ‘bro’ vibe and club events were rarely organized by leadership and club meetings were salesy,” notes Erin Trail, Altitude Multisport Club’s former president and current volunteer. “What did it for me was a no-drop group ride that the current president and coaching director were on. I had done three Ironman races, and they dropped ME. I knew the route and was fine, but I thought: ‘What if I was a upcoming person? What kind of experience would this be?’”.

Since the president was term-limited, Trail was able to step up as president in 2016 to change the atmosphere to a friendlier, more inclusive one.

“That first year was very hard. I decided to make the club more inclusive and friendly to beginners and women, eliminating sales or conflict of interest issues and improving communications,” Trail states. “I lost a LOT of club friends because I wanted to make things different. Half my board quit because they didn’t want to be held accountable. But in my first year as president, membership grew from 50 to 150 members!”.

Today, Altitude Multisport Club features winter Sunday pool swims with a coach and travel camps to Moab and a local state park in addition to regular training and racing activities.

Industry observers note that “My second term as president was much better, with a diverse board that I handpicked. We added a family membership so households, including kids, could join at a group rate,” Trail notes. “And we made it clear that the environment is welcoming, organized, and a safe space to learn for everyone.”.

It has been revealed that “A LOT of skinny white men. That’s what I saw in triathlon. I didn’t see enough women, and I really didn’t see anyone who was bigger. I realized that if I wanted to see more folks that looked like me, I had to be the coach that made triathlon a place for all folks, regardless of size, shape, color, or anything else,” states Kyla Lupo, who took things into her own hands, getting certified as a coach, learning everything she could, and starting her team, Go Big!, with just one athlete and “a bunch of friends pretending to be my team.” Since then, Go Big! has grown to 22 athletes.

In a recent development, “Our team makes a point to let folks know that they are already loved, exactly as they are. Team Go Massive! stands for a radical level of body inclusivity, both in sport and the world,” Kyla says. “On Team Go Big!, we work to overcome our fear and doubts while getting fit and ready for the start line. Anyone can tri in the body they have right now.”.

Social connection is crucial to the Go Major! community and takes the form of weekly team meetings where members from around the country learn, share their goals, ask for support, and expect accountability.

Recent findings suggest that “We are from all over the country, but there’s a Tuesday morning virtual trainer ride to further connect us. And of course we get to party together at races,” Lupo notes.

Disruptors: Alexa and Branden Scheel.

Sources indicate that people often join tri clubs to find community, only to discover that they are a small fish in a substantial sea. When you’re one of hundreds of athletes, you and your journey can get lost in the mix.

According to recent reports, “My husband, Branden, and I were part of two different teams like that. We felt like ‘just another membership,’” Alexa Scheel claims.

Recent findings suggest that so she and Branden pursued certifications from USA Triathlon and began building the kind of team they actually wanted to be part of. In 2023, the Scheels launched Branden Scheel Racing, which focuses on athlete relationships and connection. Despite being a team with athletes around the world, the Scheels strive to make their team feel like family and make each athlete feel seen.

Recent findings suggest that “If we don’t personally know something about each of the team members, we’ve grown too big, which is why we sit between 100 to 150 members. We are committed to keeping this team on the smaller side,” Scheel says. The beating heart of the team is its Facebook group, where athletes connect through monthly games and seminars, get answers to their most pressing questions, and find encouragement.

It has been revealed that “On our team, every athlete stays until the last athlete completes their event because EVERYONE deserves to have someone cheering them on at the finish line. We’ve even had 15 people stay at the finish line for the midnight finish of Ironman Arizona for one of our athletes,” Scheel says. “Having a tri family on and off course to cheer for you and celebrate one of the best days of your life is a huge part of our team culture.”.

Disruptors: Jaclyn Fahey, Tara Hofmayer, and Sami Saad.

Industry observers note that fifteen years ago, Jaclyn Fahey started a tri team through a bike store. As it evolved, Fahey recognized the need for a more affordable Long Island-based team, and Landshark Endurance was born.

Industry observers note that “It began as a pizza-and-beer team with a triathlon problem, but Tara and Sami have helped take the lead. Because both are speech therapists and have the gift of gab, they’ve attracted a lot more members,” Fahey says. The open-level, co-ed multisport team supports members of all backgrounds with educational clinics and workshops, group workouts, and of course, social events that revolve around pizza and beer.

“By sharing our passion and experiences, we hope to show young athletes that success isn’t always measured by winning, but by perseverance, sportsmanship, and the courage to try,” Fahey claims. “You don’t have to be the fastest or the strongest. You just have to show up for yourself, put in the effort, and enjoy the journey. At the end of the day, the greatest part isn’t always crossing the finish line – it’s the people who help you get there.”.

In a recent development, “I’m non-binary, and when I visit online triathlon groups and ask if there are any fellow non-binary athletes, it’s not uncommon that transphobes will flood the comments. I can only speak for myself, but the fear of discrimination, or being attacked verbally or worse, can be the most intimidating thing for non-binary and trans triathletes about tri clubs,” claims Ruth Carter, a lawyer and triathlete. “There’s so much misinformation out there about trans women and non-binary athletes, as well as assumptions that are not supported by research.”.

When Carter couldn’t find a triclub that promoted equal participation and respect, they created Mutants & Masochists, a tri club that believes in equal participation, recognition, and respect for all triathletes, and advocates for non-binary and trans triathletes.

“We’re just getting started, but I hope the club is a place where trans people can connect, both online and in real life,” Carter says.

In 2023, Hannah Bradbury was training to break an open-water swim record when she was rushed to the ER for an emergency surgery to remove her gallbladder.

It has been revealed that “My first thought when I woke up was, ‘When can I get back in the water?’ The answer was six weeks at least,” notes Bradbury, who had already lost half of her thyroid to cancer in 2017. In an attempt to be part of sport in a way that cancer or a freak surgery couldn’t disrupt, Bradbury created Chicago’s North Avenue Swim and Triathlon Yo (NASTY) Instagram account to post about swimming until she could get back in the water. She also launched book clubs and threw happy hours to create space for people to be more than just athletes, from cancer survivors to diabetic athletes striving to stay in sport on their own terms.

“Tri and swim clubs are great at training people. They’re not always great at holding onto people when they’re injured, sick, slow, starting over, or just burned out. I wanted to build a club that could hold everyone, from those winning the Chicago Triathlon to anyone rebuilding from injuries, or battling setbacks and the identity crises nobody warns you about when you’re sidelined,” notes Bradbury, who faced another cancer scare in 2023. “While I waited on the biopsy, my friends kept me distracted by doing a 100-mile ride with me, covered in glitter, that we called the ride Centuslay.”.

Fortunately, the biopsy came back negative, and the women’s century became an official NASTY tradition every fall.

It has been revealed that “Before NASTY I had a hard time making real friends with people who don’t just ask, ‘How was your swim?’ Through NASTY, I met friends who ask how they can show up for me,” Bradbury claims. “NASTY has grown to over 340 members, and through this community, people have found jobs through a swim or a random happy hour, and even fallen in love. Sport has become an accessory to our friendships, not the glue.”.

“When I first got into triathlon in 2010, I was fortunate to have a warm, welcoming entry point into the sport. My goal with the T2 community is to pay it forward so others can also ease into the sport, learn to love it, and stay connected for the long haul,” states Bryan Mewes, who opened T2 Triathlon & Cycling, a triathlon-focused bike shop in Long Beach, California, in 2023. “The biggest hurdle for beginners is usually being overwhelmed by gear. That and the open-water swim. Once they realize that the shop is a space where they can comfortably ask questions and our group is built on encouragement rather than competition, that anxiety disappears fast.”.

In a recent development, mewes explains that while it’s easy to say “everyone is welcome,” making sure someone is paired up with a partner at their pace or ensuring no one gets left behind takes actual effort that T2’s committed to making. Beyond the group rides, weekly runs, and bay swims, T2 brings people together off the course and keeps the vibe low-key and welcoming by hosting family dinners at local restaurants, beach days after races, and even a movie club.

It has been revealed that “Some people only do our social events, while others only join our rides. What matters is that they participate in their way and see themselves as part of the community. That’s the core of T2. Training is just the anchor,” Mewes says.

Disruptors: Ruth Marie Oliver and Team Rocket’s Race Directors and Officers.

Team Rocket Tri Club (TRTC) is on a mission to promote a fit and healthy lifestyle. Every month, the club organizes a themed, post-brick social, and throughout the year, it hosts various races, from a beginner-friendly pool swim to a duathlon and sprint triathlons.

It has been revealed that during the summer months, TRTC hosts Tuesday night bricks featuring a multitude of pace groups, ensuring no rider is left behind and everyone has buddies to ride with. And in the winter, the focus is on swim clinics and winter trail running.

“Our club president, Ruth Marie Oliver, has done amazing things, including growing our membership to over 300 people,” says Cynthia Mitchell, race director of TRTC’s Heel and Crank Duathlon.

To up the fun factor, TRTC has its own well-traveled bike box that members can borrow, adding their own sticker to its travel history and essentially bringing the whole team along for that athlete’s adventure. There’s also a TRTC hat that is currently “on tour.” It’s been spotted everywhere from Leeds, Alabama, to the head of Bob Babbit in Kona during the Ironman World Championship this year.

Disruptors: Corinne Geerdts Merten and Melissa Niemuth-Seamonson.

In 2019, Corinne Geerdts Merten and Melissa Niemuth-Seamonson relaunched TriBabes WI, a women’s-only, USAT-certified team, to provide a community for women of all abilities and ages to train together.

“Some women join us purely to have the chance to work out with others for one, two, or all three sports. No matter what the sport or goal, we support each other without all the egos,” Merten says. TriBabesWI makes aspects of triathlon like climbing hills, changing tires, nutrition, and making a race plan less daunting through the clinics it offers. For TriBabe’s annual team triathlon, athletes can ride with a buddy for the bike portion.

Sources indicate that team offerings aren’t limited to the swim-bike-run. There are team hikes, skiing and snowshoeing in the winter, and opportunities to volunteer and shake a cowbell for others.

“We’ve donated our time and efforts to Breakthrough T1D, USAT triathlon events in Milwaukee, Ironman Wisconsin, and naturally Girls on the Run,” Merten claims.

Recent findings suggest that “When I was upcoming to this sport, I went for a bike ride with a triathlon group and got dropped within moments,” states Topper, an author and coach who started WeREndurance in 2017. “If you’re just starting out, don’t look like everyone else, or just feel different from everyone, many clubs can feel elitist, especially when you get dropped. WeREndurance is nothing like that. It’s inclusive and diverse.”.

As the group’s triathletes grew older and more injury-prone, however, WeREndurance membership began to drop, so Topper proposed transitioning from a strictly triathlon group to a lifestyle group. Now, WeREndurance members who live locally in Long Beach, New York, can participate in monthly hikes and quarterly races, as well as pool parties, holiday parties, diner breakfasts, and even a psychic night. Members who live out of state can stay connected through monthly meditation sessions, a book club, and monthly/bi-monthly educational webinars.

“These types of activities welcome everyone, including those who are injured or on the sidelines. This builds bonds and social connections,” Topper explains. “As you get older, you realize that sport is not only about being on the podium. It’s about community and having fun with your peers. The social aspect becomes just as important as training and racing.”.

Disruptors: Brian Masayon, David Bahia, and Kristoffer Crisostomo.

In 2017, Masayon, Crisostomo, Bahia, and six of their friends formed a “silly” club to make training fun, and in doing so, others began taking notice.

Recent findings suggest that “People started reaching out, asking how to join the team. I replied that there was no team. After the 20th inquiry or so, the nine of us decided to open 3P TRI to the public as a fun, drama-free group. That was in October 2017. By the end of the year, we had over 120 members join,” Masayon states. As word spread, the nonprofit tri club’s inclusive vibe attracted members from Canada, Australia, the Philippines, and Mexico.

While Ironman race entries cost athletes between $900 and $1,200, 3P TRI has removed the financial barrier entirely, offering clinics and free 140.6-mile races that are fully supported by the team.

“There is no timing chip, so members are not pressured to prove how fast or slow they are. Instead, they train and then enjoy race day with their teammates,” Masayon indicates. For 3P’s 140.6 triathlon, members come from different states to volunteer and help their teammates finish.

According to recent reports, “People are intimidated by tri clubs because they have this impression of triathletes as being fast, quick, and strong. Our members, however, come in all shapes and sizes, and this becomes an inspiration to many people,” Masayon adds. “Nobody talks about speed and ability. We don’t play the comparison game.”.

Recent findings suggest that five years ago, a group of Latest Jersey moms tried a mud run. They had so much fun that one run turned into a road race, followed by group bike rides, and finally dipping their nail-less toes into triathlons, despite the level of intimidation.

“At a 5K, you’ll see everyone from Boston qualifiers to families participating together, sometimes with little kids in tow. Triathlons can seem like a different world from road or obstacle races. They require training and preparation across three disciplines, and the level of athleticism on display can be intimidating. Sometimes it feels like there are no actual beginners, just really accomplished athletes with super fancy bikes,” says Merino, adding that if someone shows up to ride with a mountain bike, they probably know it’s not the fastest option and don’t necessarily need unsolicited advice about upgrading. The same goes for swim form, running technique, or anything else. “If someone asks for pointers, we absolutely help them! Otherwise, the most encouraging thing we can do may be simply making them feel like they belong.”.

In a recent development, “That’s what Team Thunderclap is all about. We might not have the fanciest gear or be the fastest people, but we show up, give it everything we’ve got, and probably laugh a whole lot along the way,” Merino states. “At the end of the day, most of us aren’t competing for Olympic medals. We’re ordinary people doing extraordinary things in our spare time.”.

Fashion Has Entered Its Running Era
