Zwift’s Dedicated Indoor Bike Makes Your Winter Riding Better—and Protects Your Road Bike

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1309 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • It has been revealed that I’ve used a handful of indoor trainers over the years, but a few years ago I picked up a Wahoo Kickr Core and I thought that would be my trainer for the foreseeable future.
  • When I ran a shop, we would sell through the Wahoo Kickr Core because it has always been a product I personally love—it is easier to sell products that I genuinely believe in and use.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

It has been revealed that I’ve used a handful of indoor trainers over the years, but a few years ago I picked up a Wahoo Kickr Core and I thought that would be my trainer for the foreseeable future. It’s easy to use and reliable. It did exactly what I needed it to do—turn my bike into a trainer for offseason training.

When I ran a shop, we would sell through the Wahoo Kickr Core because it has always been a product I personally love—it is easier to sell products that I genuinely believe in and use. More than that, every shop team I’ve worked with would use the Wahoo Kickr Core as their trainer of choice. Then I was introduced to the Zwift Ride and realized I was not done buying trainers just yet.

As the shop’s service manager, I got firsthand experience assessing bikes after a season of sitting on the trainer; let alone season after season, year after year. The level of maintenance needed for those bikes was initially shocking to me as well as to the customer. Most of us are aware we need to do maintenance on our bikes that we ride outside, but it’s easy to forget about our unsung hero—our trainer bike sitting in the basement constantly covered in sweat, spilled drink mix, and getting the watts cranked into it day in and day out.

There’s a better way than just throwing your bike on the trainer for your offseason. The Zwift Ride V2 with the Wahoo Kickr Core is now my top recommended way to use a bike trainer. It’s easy to see why.

According to recent reports, for those who have multiple riders in one house, this may be one of the biggest benefits. When I had my bike set up on the Kickr Core it was harder for my wife to just hop on the trainer. Since my old trainer bike was carbon, even a simple saddle adjustment required a torque wrench. I’ve even gone so far as to change out stems to change the reach too—not the hardest thing to do, but by no means convenient. On the Zwift Ride, most fit adjustments are super easy and take just seconds.

It has been revealed that the Zwift Ride 2 I’ve been on even has multiple crank length options set up in the cranks, so you just swap the pedals to a different hole in the crank to change the effective crank length. Taking out one more friction point between me and being able to start my trainer ride means I’m even more likely to get my winter trainer miles in.

The other day I was a few minutes into my warmup and I needed to adjust my reach a bit. I pulled the integrated 6mm Allen key out from its place under the top tube, easily adjusted the reach at the handlebars, tightened everything down, and reinstalled the tool all without interrupting my cadence. Having the tool I need to adjust just about anything on the bike is a new level of convenience I was not used to.

Sources indicate that as Matt Phillips pointed out in his Zwift Ride 2 review, “Mechanically, the Ride is almost primitive.” For clarity, this is by no means a negative—when it comes to a trainer bike, mechanically primitive but extremely functional is a best-case scenario. This bike has a chain that goes from the chainring, through a chain tensioner, around the Zwift Cog attached to the Wahoo Kickr, and back up to the chainring. There’s no derailleur, no front tire that needs air, no brakes to knock out of alignment. The handlebars don’t even turn, so there’s no headset to replace in the spring because it was sitting in a pool with sweat all winter.

On the other side, you’re saving your daily driver from a lot of unseen mechanical damage. As the snow thaws out on the roads, road riders are ready to get back in the saddle under the sun, but if you use your bike on the trainer all winter, it may need A LOT of love before it’s road-worthy.

In a recent development, A bike that sits on the trainer all winter collects significant corrosion in headset and bottom bracket bearings. The sweat that comes off your head drops straight onto your headset and sweat from your body (and any of those sticky drink mixes) drop straight down toward the bottom bracket. Then we get to the drivetrain. I’ve had bikes come in around March that need full drivetrain replacement: chainrings, cassette, and chain after a good season of indoor miles. Finally, we get to the handlebar—at a minimum you should replace that bar tape after a season riding on the trainer. This also gives you a chance to get the handlebar looked at to make sure all that corrosion (sweat) hasn’t eaten into the them.

I’ve seen service tickets range anywhere from $100 to almost a thousand dollars just to get a bike off the trainer and ready to ride outside. For some people one season of trainer riding on the Zwift Ride 2 could be more cost-effective than using your road bike on a trainer.

Sources indicate that before an activity becomes a habit people are good at finding reasons not to do something. It doesn’t take long to setup a bike on the Wahoo Kickr Core, but even that little bit of set up time to pop your bike on the trainer is one more hurdle for you not to ride today. If you have to swap your cassette over from your bike to the trainer—you can almost forget about it.

In a recent development, it doesn’t just go for getting your bike on the trainer. This week in Pennsylvania we’re having a stretch of perfect riding weather—relatively low humidity, sunny, and temperatures between 55 degrees and 60 degrees. Next week’s forecast calls for colder temperatures and rain, also known as great indoor-riding weather. But this week, if I have a window of time to ride, I want to be able to just hop on my bike and go; I don’t want to have to take the bike off the trainer and reinstall my cassette before I can even start pedaling outside. With a dedicated trainer setup, I can just take my bike off the hook on the wall and roll away. Next week, when the weather goes south, I can just hop back on the trainer.

The Zwift Ride makes it easier to do things like use power-ups, steer the avatar, and toggle through screens, but those features are just an added bonus compared to the other reasons to pick one up. It is a burly, simple, near-flawless machine for riding on the trainer. It’s stable when putting out your max watts. The built-in tool makes it easy to accommodate different riders—including adjusting the reach. Even the bottle cages are designed to fit almost any bottle. The bike’s handlebar tray fits an iPad or other tablet well, but I pair it with a rolling trainer table if I’m using my laptop. You can buy the Zwift Ride itself, or as a package deal with Wahoo’s excellent Kickr Core 2, which gives you everything you need for a stress-free indoor riding season.

Jason Griffin is Bicycling's Senior Health and Fitness Editor, bringing more than a decade of fitness experience and years in the cycling industry to every story. A former personal trainer and bike shop manager, he's lined up for crits, tackled enduros, but prefers getting lost on multi-day bikepacking adventures. Lately though, his toughest balancing act has been fitting trainer rides between family life and the next adventure.

Industry News: The 8 Best Treadmills of 2026

💡 Key Takeaways

  • It has been revealed that there are a ton of treadmills on the market right now, and they’re better than they’ve ever been.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, we earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

Sources indicate that before you get on the treadmill hate train, hear me out. They can save your training, and I swear, they can be a ton of fun—really. Between the engaging, interactive streaming treadmill classes, and the ability to strip down to your skivvies and have no one see you sweat, it’s the perfect accompaniment to your marathon training, interval workouts, and even steady, zone 2 workouts. All from the comfort of your own home. And did you know that with many insurance plans, you can pay for your treadmill with FSA dollars? That’s a solid fiscal choice, right there.

It has been revealed that there are a ton of treadmills on the market right now, and they’re better than they’ve ever been. They have more features, use less electricity, and are more versatile than ever before. Some are virtually personal trainers in and of themselves.

In a recent development, we’re in the process of testing a few new models, and we’ve just added the Urevo CyberMega, which is the first treadmill designed specifically for marathon training. It’s pretty freaking sick, I cannot lie.

Looking for a more heavy-duty treadmill that can handle higher speeds, longer miles, and more complex training plans? See our guide for the best advanced treadmills, which cost more but offer more training features and sturdier builds.

There’s really something special about this machine. The NordicTrack Commercial 1750 treadmill hits that “Goldilocks-level” sweet spot with its cushioning—it’s responsive enough to save your joints without making your run feel like a slog or an unstable adventure. And with a 60-inch belt, even our tallest testers with their gazelle-like strides had plenty of room to stretch out and feel steady.

According to recent reports, our testers absolutely gushed over the treadmill’s sleek, streamlined design, especially the Z-shaped console with its high-perched 16-inch screen. It’s perfectly positioned for runners who like to stay close to the controls. While we wished the cup holders were a bit deeper for our oversized water bottles, the slim arms offered a surprisingly stable grip, even when our hands got a little… enthusiastic.

The 1750’s speed adjustments are pretty standard, going from 6 mph to a zippy 12 mph in 8 seconds. This is totally fine for 400- to 800-meter training, but for intense, quick-pickup speedwork, it’s not quite as snappy as some might like. Our testers did note one minor peeve: the lack of quick keys for 10 and 11 mph.

Industry observers note that we practically insist you dive into NordicTrack’s iFit program for an out-of-this-world experience. Our testers found its ability to read and adjust their runs to be nothing short of revolutionary during testing. While the high horsepower motor and Bluetooth speakers do make the machine a bit boisterous, it’s not at all distracting when you’re walking with your headphones on.

According to recent reports, despite its daunting price tag, the 1750 is a total workhorse that will supercharge your runs—and it goes on sale often. The built-in Netflix feature is a godsend, making miles absolutely fly by, and that cushioning is pure magic for your joints. Bottom line: the NordicTrack Commercial 1750 is a fantastic all-around package and a top-notch investment for most runners.

NordicTrack Commercial 1750 Review.

The Horizon T101 treadmill proves you don’t need a huge budget for a fantastic workout. At a sale price of just $600, this compact folding machine impressed us with consistent performance over weeks of testing. It’s a low-to-the-ground, 20- by 55-inch deck, ideal for casual runners 6 feet and under.

In a recent development, the T101 boasts a three-zone running surface, offering extra cushioning where you land, less where you toe off, and a smooth transition in between for a supremely comfortable, low-impact ride. While it skips the fancy screens, its functionality shines. Connect to Strava or Peloton, or dive into workouts and courses via the free atZone app. Plus, there’s a perfect spot for your iPad to stream your favorite highlights!

The six built-in programs are straightforward, displaying calories burned, heart rate, distance, speed, and incline (up to 10 percent). While it can hit a 6-minute mile, be mindful: the speed and incline dials are sensitive—one haptic notch, not a full spin, increases your pace.

In a recent development, but you know what’s a real showstopper? The T101’s incredibly easy, one-step hydraulic fold. Just lift the back, and it zips up. To release, toe the center bar, and it gently lowers itself.

For its price, the T101’s features are unbeatable. It’s not for marathoners or speed demons, but for everyone else, it’s a solid win.

Horizon’s 7.0 folding treadmill is a robust upgrade, boasting a spacious 60-inch deck perfect for long strides, though its 20-inch width might feel snug if your mind wanders. Cushioning is excellent for long runs, but expect some bounce when the incline exceeds 5 percent—so perhaps skip the speedy hill work.

It has been revealed that this machine is on the bulkier side, resembling a gym-quality unit, but its integrated features ensure easy setup. We loved the eye-level tablet holder, making streaming a breeze. Below, you’ll find a digital/manual console, fan, Bluetooth speakers, and two generously wide (if shallow) cup holders with room for your essentials.

Recent findings suggest that programming-wise, the 7.0 shines with its ability to link to Peloton, Apple Watch, and Samsung Galaxy watches, displaying calories and distance directly. Peloton classes synced smoothly, making transitions seamless.

It has been revealed that A standout feature: knobs on the grips allow for effortless pace adjustments without breaking your stride. While there’s a subtle lag when decreasing speed, it’s barely noticeable at top speeds.

Industry observers note that at around $1,000 on sale, this treadmill offers impressive value. Its blend of convenience and comfort makes it a winner. Pro tip: opt for white-glove delivery—this beast is heavy, and assembly is a pain!

Full Horizon 7.0 AT Treadmill Review.

Sources indicate that marathon training demands months of relentless mileage, a crap ton of structured workouts, and more consistency than most of us think we’re capable of. The Urevo CyberMega is a treadmill that claims to be built specifically for the rigors of that beast of blocks. In a market crowded with all-purpose machines designed to serve everyone from casual walkers to occasional joggers to high-mileage baddies, the CyberMega is thinking of the needs of marathon runners first.

According to recent reports, that marathon-focused idea makes the entire experience. Rather than treating running as just one feature among many, the CyberMega is designed around the realities of high-volume training. According to the brand, every aspect of the machine is intended to support athletes preparing for long-distance races, making it a notably different proposition from traditional fitness-focused treadmills.

According to recent reports, there are marathon courses built into the app that control your ‘mill, there’s AI coaching to get you to your PR, and a fun competitive leaderboard where you are up against other users. This treadmill is made to keep your training going when you can’t get outside and also? To keep it exciting. It is honestly fairly impressive and a ton of fun to run on.

Industry observers note that I was also impressed by how smooth the run is and how compact the machine is. It folds easily, stores without much hassle, and feels dang streamlined for a treadmill made to support hardcore training. That’s also the biggest drawback. If you’re over 6 feet tall, this is not the ‘mill for you with a 52-inch-long deck. But in spite of the short deck, it landed on this list is because it’s a wide-open area that doesn’t feel impeded by the bars.

The rotary knob is another nifty feature. It’s simple, responsive, and super convenient during workouts, and has speed and incline adjustments feeling smoother and more intuitive than traditional button-based controls or rocker dials. Overall, if you’re gonna be a world major chaser, you might want to think about chasing them on this ‘mill.

Got a few runners in the family, or you’re a high-mileage runner? The NordicTrack 2450 is a seriously solid folding treadmill that’s got your back. It’s built tough, has great cushioning, and a huge 22-by-60-inch running surface, so you can just run without worrying about comfort and stability.

The Z-shaped handlebar and crossbar design are super minimalist, keeping the console right there when you need it, and giving you plenty of room to stretch out at the front of the belt.

You’ve got your standard speed and incline adjustments, and this baby can zoom from 6 to 14 mph in under 10 seconds—perfect for those quick interval bursts. It has those quick keys like the 1750, but sometimes it can be a little tricky to nail down specific speeds.

It has been revealed that where the NordicTrack really shines is its iFit programming. We’re talking thousands of workouts, even marathon courses! Yeah, it’s an extra cost, but seriously, it’s a huge motivator. And that big display? It’s awesome. You can pause your run to squeeze in some strength training or even stream your favorite shows.

Sources indicate that fair warning, though: putting this thing together is a beast, so you might want to call in a pro. And while it’s not super loud, it might be a bit disruptive if you’re trying to sneak in an early morning workout while everyone else is still snoozing.

Industry observers note that the ProForm Carbon TLX is a robust and dependable treadmill, designed for those who appreciate solid performance over excessive features. Its simplicity allows for focused workouts, minimizing distractions so you can stay in tune with your run. While it offers connectivity for phones, tablets, and fitness apps like iFit, at its core, the Carbon TLX is a workhorse—a no-fuss machine ready for you to hop on, get your miles in, and hop off.

According to recent reports, the treadmill features a responsive and cushioned surface that offers a pleasant bounce at higher speeds. Our testers found that despite the softer feel, the generous 60- by 20-inch deck allowed for a natural stride. However, I did occasionally feel myself drawing closer to the front console, so if you prefer more forward space, a different model might be better suited.

It has been revealed that for speed enthusiasts, the Carbon TLX is a dream. It rapidly reaches its top speed of 12 mph, and manual buttons provide smooth transitions between speeds. The incline goes up to 12 percent, providing a challenging workout that feels surprisingly good, even uphill. A standout feature is the powerful fan, strategically placed to provide excellent airflow—a detail any woman who’s done the “lift the boobs to get air” maneuver will appreciate.

If you’re a first-time treadmill buyer or looking to stay within budget, the Carbon TLX offers exceptional value for its price.

Recent findings suggest that the Bowflex T9 treadmill brings a punch of fun and functionality to home workouts, making it a standout pick for casual runners and fitness fans alike. The red center line on the belt isn’t just for show—it helps wandering runners stay in their lane, so every jog feels more confident (and a little less wobbly). The running surface is firm and comfortable, with just enough pep to keep things lively, while the compact, foldable design slides neatly out of the way after your workout adventure.

The controls and incline? Well, they’re not winning any races. Adjustments take their time, so interval chasers might grumble about holding down those buttons like they’re cranking up a jack-in-the-box. But the T9 redeems itself with robust app compatibility—it syncs up with Peloton, Zwift, and even Apple Watch for gadget lovers, and has an oversized tablet holder for serious streaming or stats-watching mid-run.

It has been revealed that weighing in with a 350-pound weight capacity, a quiet motor, and speed toggles at your fingertips, this treadmill turns everyday training into smooth sailing. It may not be a speed demon, but the T9’s thoughtful features combine comfort and tech for an overall enjoyable ride.

Sources indicate that the Echelon Stride 6 is the treadmill I’ve kept at home after running over 1,200 miles on dozens of machines testing them for this article. It’s a solid, foldable treadmill that fits well in small spaces without feeling cramped. The larger-than-expected deck is 20.5 by 60 inches, giving plenty of room for a natural stride, even at my height of 6 feet. The deck provides firm cushioning that’s comfortable but not overly soft, which I definitely prefer for a closer to road-like feel.

The fold-flat design is a major bonus. The mill is stupid easy to tuck away under a bed or stand upright in a closet or—how I do it—up against a wall behind a curtain. That said, it’s heavy when folded upright, so moving it alone can be a pain. The treadmill has a powerful built-in fan and heart rate sensors, nice extras for longer sessions.

Overall, the Stride 6 isn’t flashy or cushioned like some high-end models, but it delivers a dependable run and great space-saving convenience. For a runner who values a firm deck, quiet motor, and compact footprint, it’s a practical choice that keeps me coming back.

Recent findings suggest that not everyone needs a treadmill for running, and we get that. Sometimes, what you need is access to movement and the ability to stay active all day long. Enter the Go Plus under-desk walking pad. It is the bridge between daily life and running.

It has been revealed that I love using this walking pad when I am working. It’s calm and quiet, but allows me to keep my body and brain active when I'd otherwise be sedentary. It has a deck that is a wonderful size to fit under your standing desk, though I do think it could be just a teeny bit wider. It’s only about 50 pounds, and has wheels so you can maneuver it around your space easily. It’s remote-controlled for easy use, and best of all? You can store this gal vertically in your closet. (Just don’t forget about it in there!).

According to recent reports, each and every treadmill on this list has been thoroughly evaluated by our team of editors at Runner’s World. I have personally tested each and every ‘mill on this list. Additionally, we solicited input from other staff at our office, like News Editor Theo Kahler, who has a PR of 14:20 in the 5K.

It has been revealed that the team and I evaluated each treadmill, running for miles in every conceivable combination of uses. We evaluated how they feel, how well they change speeds and inclines, and even how they sound when they’re running. I then gauged that performance against their prices, customer service, and setup and delivery.On that note: I know that not everyone who runs is going to be able to move around a piece of equipment that weighs hundreds of pounds. As someone with a partially paralyzed left hand, I cannot handle the setup and assembly of a treadmill, so good customer service is a highly key factor. I want to make sure that you’re not just getting a good ’mill, but a good overall experience.

Apart from general treadmill safety, there are a few questions you need to ask yourself before you buy the treadmill. These include how you want to use it, how long your stride is, if you want entertainment or training built in, and what you need as far as weight limits are concerned.

Recent findings suggest that having a comfortable treadmill means having one with a deck large enough to suit your stride. You don’t want to feel like you’re chasing to stay near the bar and not slip off the back, and you should ensure it’s wide enough that you can shake into your run without concern that you’ll step off the belt.

According to recent reports, having a running surface at least 20 inches wide is the bare minimum, and only for runners and walkers who have a consistent gait and few distractions when they run. It’s great for space to have a slimmer belt, but like running on a narrow trail, it requires concentration.

Sources indicate that the length of the deck is a trickier problem. What you need is largely dependent on the length of your stride, where you like to land in relation to your center of gravity, and your height/limb length. Having a deck that is too short puts you at risk for falling. Alternatively, it might have you trying to run up against the bar, which can affect your cadence and speed work, as you are essentially trying to outrun the machine instead of following its speed.

Industry observers note that if you’re planning on using the treadmill for running, you’re going to want at least 55 inches of deck length. If you’re just using it for walking, 45 to 50 inches should suffice.

If you’ve ever uttered the word “fartlek” out loud, you, my friend, need a treadmill that has easily adjustable speeds, and many of them at that. Do you need it to go all the way up to 12 miles per hour (generally the fastest speed on any treadmill) to hit that 5-minute mile? Probably not, but you at least want it to hit your top speed, and you want it to do it smoothly and easily.

Running is a sport of efficiency, and having to stop just to punch buttons that are not immediately responsive or are difficult to find will take away from your training.

Incline training is great for a lot of reasons, not least of which is preparing to run a hilly course. The majority of commercial treadmills offer some level of incline capability. Higher end models can reach a maximum of a 15 degree incline, designed to test the limits of your quads and glutes. Some models also give you the ability to do the opposite—offering decline modes—but those are pretty rare.

According to recent reports, treadmills offer more programming and entertainment than ever. Treadmills are no longer just a belt, motor, and bar. They are now Wi-Fi-compatible machines with programming capable of creating entire running prepares and helping you execute them.

On-board systems like NordicTrack’s iFit are designed to help runners (and walkers) on their journey by providing them with tools like heart-rate monitor based workouts, whole-body fitness programs for runners, and responsive tech that monitors intensity, adjusting for your needs as you go.

Recent findings suggest that and perhaps more importantly for many of us, a lot of treadmills can connect to streaming services like Netflix, Spotify, Hulu, and more. Nothing will get you running quite so fast as watching Annabelle while you’re hitting your miles (though it may artificially elevate your heart rate, causing the machine to tell you to slow down).

Motors are a critical element to the design and function of the treadmill. There are typically two motors on each treadmill—one for running the belt and one to power the incline. The motor running the belt is the one taking the heaviest damage and using the greatest amount of energy, so it needs to be robust.

Speed and motors are closely related—in order to give the user an option to hit higher speeds, the treadmill needs a strong motor to keep up. Most motors are between 1.5 and 4 horsepower. We should note that the majority of treadmills with higher weight limits (north of 300 pounds) tend to have higher horsepower.

We have found in our testing that higher-power motors can also take a lot more abuse, staying right and ready for more miles. Unfortunately, this does typically mean that the treadmill itself may be more expensive, but for larger-bodied individuals, distance runners, or speed runners, it’s worth the cost of admission.

What are the potential benefits for walking or running on a treadmill versus outdoors?

It’s predictable. Greer notes that it “allows the runner to precisely set and control all parameters, including speed, incline, and duration. This is especially beneficial for walkers or runners who are systematically progressing back into activity, either after injury, time away, latest to running, or runners completing a specific workout.”.

It also helps you stay consistent, which is critical when training. “Given the benefits of accessibility and predictability, a treadmill can help to promote a more consistent exercise routine.”.

What are some of the potential risks of treadmill training/use?

Sources indicate that there are risks for specific treadmill injuries. “Recent literature shows some differences in biomechanics between running on a treadmill vs overground. Differences in biomechanics result in tissues being loaded differently, specifically increased loading of the Achilles tendon with treadmill running.”.

In a recent development, when you run outdoors, your body encounters different obstacles that help strengthen it. “Walking/running on the treadmill does not allow the diversification of movements and muscle activity required in comparison to outdoor walking/running. For example, up/down hills, turning, stepping onto curb or over puddle.”.

In a recent development, you might exert yourself more. There is evidence to suggest that “runners report a higher rate of perceived exertion (RPE) when running on a treadmill vs overground.”.

You need to know yourself and your limits to be safe. “Treadmills allow the walker/runner to easily increase the belt speed, however, make sure the speed does not exceed that which you are able to run safe and that you can continue to run with your normal running mechanics.”.

Tips for safe treadmill training?

Treadmills are a major piece of exercise equipment, and they can be dangerous if not installed properly and monitored when in use. That is why we spoke with Ed Pryts, chief sales officer at Gym Source, a 30-year treadmill industry veteran, to learn the most vital safety factors before you purchase a fresh treadmill for your home.

In a recent development, cat Bowen, senior editor of commerce; reviews, is a seasoned runner with more than 20 years of distance running experience, including dozens of marathons, half marathons, and even a few ultra marathons. For over a decade, she has tested parenting, fitness, home, and running gear and written in-depth guides to help readers with their next purchase. Holding multiple advanced degrees and right now studying kinesiology, Cat Bowen brings research-backed insight to all of her guides. Passionate about women’s health and neurodivergent inclusion, she advocates for closing research gaps and helping others—especially AudHD people—find joy in running and fitness.

Jeff is Runner-in-Chief for Runner’s World and the director of product testing. He has tested and reviewed running shoes, GPS watches, headphones, apparel, and more for nearly two decades. He regularly tests more than 100 pairs of shoes each year, and once had a 257-day streak running in different models. Jeff can usually be found on the roads, racing anything from the mile to a marathon, but he also enjoys racing up mountains and on snowshoes. When he’s not running, you’ll probably find him hanging from a ladder making repairs and renovations to his house (he’s also director of product testing for Popular Mechanics).

3 Winter Fueling Mistakes You’re Probably Making—and How to Fix Them

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1307 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that for many runners, winter presents a greater challenge than other seasons when it comes to fueling.
  • As we approach the start of winter, it’s a good time to check in on your nutrition habits and make tweaks to set you up for stronger running through the season.
  • Three registered dietitians, who have years of competitive athletic experience themselves, share the most common fueling mistakes they see runners make this time of year and explain exactly how to fix each one.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that for many runners, winter presents a greater challenge than other seasons when it comes to fueling. Our regular eating schedules shift around social gatherings, holiday menus influence our usual food choices, and staying hydrated can take more effort without higher temperatures to drive our thirst.

As we approach the start of winter, it’s a good time to check in on your nutrition habits and make tweaks to set you up for stronger running through the season.

Three registered dietitians, who have years of competitive athletic experience themselves, share the most common fueling mistakes they see runners make this time of year and explain exactly how to fix each one.

It has been revealed that vitamin D deficiencies are common among athletes in winter, Maddie Alm, RD, a registered dietitian and the founder of Fueling Forward Sports Nutrition in Colorado, tells Runner’s World. That’s because shorter days and colder temperatures can mean less exposure to the sun’s UVB rays, which help our bodies produce vitamin D.

Alm explains that this vitamin not only supports strong bones, but also helps keep our immune and digestive systems functioning at their best. It plays an key role in brain health and mood, too. According to the National Institutes of Health, low blood levels of the vitamin have been associated with a higher risk of depression.

The Fix: Get outside daily to catch some sunshine, and focus on eating more vitamin D–rich foods, with the goal to consume 600 international units (IU) per day.

Good sources of vitamin D include milk, yogurt, cottage cheese, tuna, salmon, egg yolk, and mushrooms. Some cereals and orange juices are also vitamin D–fortified. For reference, three ounces of salmon contain 450 IU, one cup of cow’s milk contains 180 IU, one large egg yolk contains 40 IU, and one cup of fortified cereal contains 40 IU.

It’s a good idea, Alm adds, to check your levels through bloodwork once or twice a year and to consult a professional if your numbers come back low. If you have a hard time hitting your daily quota through food alone, you may benefit from taking a vitamin D supplement.

According to recent reports, runners can also overlook vitamin C intake this time of year, notes Sakiko Minagawa, RD, a registered dietitian for the Division of Sports Medicine at Nationwide Children’s Hospital in Ohio and two-time Olympic Marathon Trials qualifier. Vitamin C, also called ascorbic acid, supports immune health, which is especially vital during cold and flu season.

Recent findings suggest that our bodies also need vitamin C to produce collagen, a protein that’s essential for tissue growth and repair. “While vitamin C may not prevent you from outright getting sick, some research reveals that it may decrease the duration of cold symptoms,” Minagawa explains.

According to recent reports, the Fix: Up your consumption of foods with vitamin C, such as bell peppers, citrus fruits, greens, and strawberries. Women should aim for 75 milligrams per day, while men should aim for 90 milligrams daily.

You’ll get about 210 milligrams from one large red or orange bell pepper, and 90 milligrams in a cup of raw strawberry halves—each of which achieves your recommended daily dose.

According to recent reports, because vitamin C helps with iron absorption, Minagawa suggests pairing the two whenever possible. Some meals she recommends are a spinach salad with strawberries, an omelet with spinach and red bell peppers, and tomato soup with lentils or black beans.

In a recent development, in the winter, you might not end your run with a dry mouth and sweat-soaked shirt like in the summer, but it’s still critical to hydrate. “Even when it’s cold, you still sweat,” claims Minagawa, which means you still need to replenish fluids throughout the day, as well as before and after a workout.

Sources indicate that similarly, your midrun fueling and hydrating remain just as crucial for performance. It’s true: Tearing open an energy gel with gloved hands can pose a real challenge. But, if you’re doing long runs through the colder months, you still need to consume enough carbohydrates during your effort.

The Fix: Minagawa suggests carrying a water bottle that you can easily drink from and refill throughout the day. If you have a hard time sipping on plain water, remember that soups, broths, and hot chocolate can also help you stay hydrated—and can double as recovery fuel.

Don’t forget about fresh fruits and vegetables, either, as they can help with hydration. Some great in-season options that can contribute to your overall fluid intake include grapefruit, clementines, pomegranate, kiwi, squash, Brussels sprouts, sweet potatoes, pears, kale, and cabbage.

Recent findings suggest that during your winter long runs, experiment with fueling options other than energy gels and chews. Some great alternatives you can easily carry in a small plastic baggie include salted Medjool dates, boiled red potatoes, dried fruit, pretzels, and even candy.

Bad weather conditions, scant daylight hours, and more limited racing opportunities make winter a time for many athletes to dial back their training. Taking an off-season can benefit you in the long haul, but Minagawa encourages runners to still stay active—even if that means swapping some runs for walks, bike rides, easy swims, or elliptical sessions.

Industry observers note that you don’t want to depart from those year-round healthy habits, Brianna Butler, RD, a registered dietitian, co-owner of Stef & Bri Wellness in Texas, and former professional WNBA athlete, previously told Runner’s World. The same applies to your nutrition.

“The biggest mistake runners make is that, when it’s the off-season, they’re off everything—they say, ‘I’m not doing anything, I’m going to eat whatever’—they’re just winging it,” Butler says. “It shouldn’t be all or nothing. We want to make sure we’re nourishing our bodies well year-round.”.

If your training load changes significantly, pay closer attention to your hunger cues to make sure your nutrition matches your energy needs.

The Fix: Maintain a daily exercise routine you enjoy, prioritize nutrient-dense meals and snacks, and resist making drastic changes to your diet.

It has been revealed that if you do find yourself feeling sluggish this time of year, it can be tempting to repent with cleanses, detoxes, and extreme exercise regimens. But such quick fixes rarely pay off in the long run, Alm warns, as they put you at risk for injury, burnout, and subpar seasons to come.

Alm notes not to stress if you ditched your typical eating and training schedule for a few weeks and are feeling less energetic as a result. When you return to your usual healthy habits, your body will naturally find its sweet spot. “Trust the process and don’t panic,” Alm advises, because our bodies may change as we move through different training phases. “It is okay to not be at your leanest year-round.”.

Sources indicate that the smartest path forward? Do your best to move your body daily, fuel it with what it needs, and give yourself permission to rest when you’re tired. That way, you’ll find yourself feeling strong and ready to train hard again come spring.

Sources indicate that morgan is a gear editor who has been with Runner’s World since 2017. She started as an intern ghostwriting The Warmup, a bygone version of the daily RW newsletter. Now, she tests and reviews anything you might find on runners’ feet-from crew socks and compression boots to carbon-plated super shoes.

A lifelong runner and shoe geek, Morgan has been chasing the perfect pair of kicks since she joined her grade school cross-country team. Since then, she ran as a Division I walk-on for the cross-country and track & field teams at the University of Delaware, where she studied English and Biology. She has one full marathon under her belt, and has raced more halfs and 5Ks than she can count.

The moment that QSuite door closes, you'll understand exactly why. If you're willing to invest the time to find availability and build your miles intentionally, this redemption is entirely within reach — and the payoff is extraordinary.

Sources indicate that if aa.com does not show availability, search the same route on Qatar's own website using a Privilege Club account. Qatar sometimes releases space that AA's system takes 24-48 hours to reflect. If you find space on Qatar but not AA, check back the following day.

Not all Qatar business class flights operate QSuites. Check the aircraft type listed in the search results — A350-1000 and select 777-300ERs have QSuites. Verify on SeatGuru or Qatar's fleet page to ensure you are booking the premium product.

Industry observers note that once you confirm QSuites availability, complete the booking on aa.com using your AAdvantage miles. The process is the same as booking any AA award flight. You will see the mileage cost plus taxes and fees before confirming.

Industry observers note that after booking through AA, manage your reservation on qatarairways.com to select your QSuites seat. Choose a window suite for maximum privacy or center suites for the Buddy Suite experience with a travel companion.

American Airlines charges approximately 70,000 AAdvantage miles one-way for business class from the US to Doha on Qatar Airways-operated flights. Taxes and fees are typically $30 to $80. A round trip comes to roughly 140,000 miles total plus minimal fees.

Both options cost roughly 70,000 points one-way. The main differences are earning sources and booking experience. AAdvantage miles are earned through Citi cards and Bilt, while Avios can be earned through Chase, Amex, Capital One, Citi, and Bilt. AA offers web booking while BA may require phone calls. Check availability through both programs — they sometimes see different award space.

Yes. The Citi AAdvantage Platinum Select earns bonus miles on purchases, Bilt Rewards transfers to AAdvantage at 1:1, AA's SimplyMiles program earns miles on everyday purchases linked to your credit card, and the AAdvantage shopping portal earns miles at online retailers. You can accumulate 70,000 or more miles without taking a single AA flight.

Recent findings suggest that airlines control how much award inventory they release to each partner. Qatar may release seats to BA's Avios program but not to AA, or vice versa. AA's search engine also has known inconsistencies with partner availability display. Always cross-reference qatarairways.com and ba.com if aa.com shows no availability on your desired dates.

This sweet spot was last verified over 90 days ago. Award availability and pricing may have changed — verify current rates before booking.

Sources indicate that using AAdvantage miles for Qatar business class is one of the strongest partner award redemptions in the oneworld alliance. At 70,000 miles for a product that retails at $5,000 to $8,000, the value per mile is outstanding. The web-based booking experience on aa.com removes the friction of phone calls, and the lack of fuel surcharges keeps your cash outlay minimal. If you earn AAdvantage miles through Citi cards or Bilt transfers, this should be at the top of your aspirational redemption list. Search early, stay flexible on dates, and book the moment QSuites space appears.

#148384. Bicycling’s Gear of the Year 2027

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 15m • 📚 Deep Dive (3047 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Bicycling ↗ Open Full Page

Bicycling’s Gear of the Year 2027

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (3047 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • There’s no shortage of latest cycling gear promising to make your bike lighter, faster, or more comfortable.
  • Our editors bring different perspectives to testing.
  • According to recent reports, our picks reflect that range of experience and the different ways we ride.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There’s no shortage of latest cycling gear promising to make your bike lighter, faster, or more comfortable. Over the past year, our editors have put those promises to the test on road and gravel rides, mountain bike trails, commutes, and in the workshop. For Gear of the Year, we’ve chosen the products that stood out most: the ones that solved a problem, made a ride more enjoyable, or delivered tangible performance that impressed us enough to recommend to you.

Our editors bring different perspectives to testing. Matt Phillips has tested bikes and gear for 30 years and has ridden more bikes than any other cycling journalist on the planet. Tara Seplavy has led product development at global bike brands, while Dan Chabanov has won national and elite titles in cyclocross and crit racing. Nearly all of us have worked in or managed bike shops.

According to recent reports, our picks reflect that range of experience and the different ways we ride. This year, we’ve organized them by price to make it easier to find something that fits your budget, whether you’re looking for a small upgrade or considering a bigger purchase. Whatever you choose, if it’s on this list, we think it will improve your ride.

Under $100 $100 to $300 $300 to $1,000 $1,000+.

I get the skepticism about a product that seems to have figured out a problem that’s existed forever, but trust me, the Tyre Glider has made me completely rethink how I install tires. Instead of fighting the final few inches with my thumbs, you simply hook it under the bead and glide it around the rim. Until you use it, it just doesn’t make sense how simple and easy it is.

Recent findings suggest that that mechanical advantage is especially useful with tight road tires and tubeless setups, where a conventional tire lever can feel precarious with carbon rims and spokes. It won’t replace a traditional lever for every job, but for the problem it’s designed to solve, it does it really well.

Last summer ended with me sporting a very prominent helmet vent hole tan line on my forehead. The reason was obvious: I avoided applying sunscreen there because every formula would sweat into my eyes. This summer I set out to find one that worked.

When I found Pelotan, I was skeptical of something marketed specifically to cyclists, but it works incredibly well. Although expensive, I found the 6-ounce bottle lasted me the entire season. It goes on light, evaporates quickly, smells nice, and most importantly doesn’t sting my eyes so I actually end up wearing it.

Industry observers note that I often ride without gloves, so I’m picky about grips. After testing both the regular and fat versions of Ergon’s GDH Team, they’ve become my favorites for any bike built to get rowdy. The rubber is pleasantly soft and tacky, providing a secure hold with bare or gloved hands. Subtle fins under the fingers help keep my hands in place without forcing me to squeeze the bars hard.

Knipex Pliers Wrench (86 03 180).

Knipex makes some of the most enjoyable to use tools we have in the Bicycling workshop. The Pliers Wrench might look like an oddly shaped adjustable wrench, but its parallel jaws provide superior clamping force. It grips hardware securely without any slipping and marring.

In a recent development, these aren't bicycle-specific tools; they’re exceptionally good tools that happen to be incredibly useful around a bike. It comes in a range of sizes, but the 7 1/4-inch is the sweet spot: compact enough to live in a bike toolbox while still opening wide enough to handle most of the jobs I throw at it.

According to recent reports, A front light is an easy addition to your road or gravel bike, but finding one that fits neatly on your cockpit can be tricky. Lezyne’s Road Drive 500 solves that problem with a slim, 75-gram body that tucks discreetly under a computer mount.

Industry observers note that despite its small size, the light offers a 500-lumen daytime flash and a 400-lumen mode for seeing the road or bike path after sunset. The replaceable battery lasts up to 55 hours in daytime flash mode or 4.5 hours in the 150-lumen enduro mode. Some computer mounts don’t let you adjust the beam's direction, but Lezyne includes a GoPro-style mount that lets you aim the light where you need it, at the expense of making the overall form factor a little less stealthy.

Peak Design Mobile Crossbody Multi-Strap.

In a recent development, as a photographer and cyclist, I’m always looking for easier ways to carry cameras while riding. Peak Design’s Mobile Crossbody Multi Strap has become a useful way to keep small cameras and accessories secure and within reach.

Its mini quick-release mechanism lets me attach anchors to multiple devices and swap between them swiftly. I’ve used it to carry a small gimbal camera while shooting the Philly Bike Race and as an added layer of security for cameras tucked into my pockets on rides. It’s also handy when traveling, letting me keep my phone or headphones tethered while making my way through an airport.

According to recent reports, spur Cycle’s R-Pro mirror gives road and gravel riders a simple way to see what’s happening behind them. Its alloy body and glass mirror have a high-end feel that looks at home even on a pricey carbon race bike, and it installs in just a few minutes.

I find it especially useful in heavy traffic, when a radar can be constantly pinging with notifications. A quick glance at the mirror helps me judge the distance to the vehicles behind me. It’s also handy on group rides to check that the person following me is still on my wheel. While the mirror doesn’t replace a radar, it never needs charging or pairing to a head unit.

I have found these Campagnolo 03 rotors to be categorically better than both SRAM and Shimano rotors while also being cheaper (a rare feat for a Campagnolo product).

It has been revealed that the main concern I have with both SRAM and Shimano’s high-end road rotors is that after hard braking, they absorb enough heat to deform and briefly make noise. Riding the same roads after switching to Campagnolo rotors? No noise after hard braking. To me, this indicates the Campagnolo rotors manage braking heat better, which gives me more confidence in their performance; plus, silence is golden. At this point, I have replaced both Shimano and SRAM rotors with these Campagnolo ones and can recommend them highly as a better rotor alternative for any road bike groupset.

Back in 2025, I bumped into an old friend at Sea Otter. He was walking around with what might be the most curious saddle prototype I’ve ever seen. It looked like it was made from plastic and Styrofoam. It was also crazy light and, according to him, fully rideable.

Now, I finally have the production version. It’s still crazy light (146g on my scale). And those funky rails? An absolute joy to use. It’s such a simple solution: the saddle slides into the clamp instead of needing to partially take everything apart in some cases. But more importantly, as someone who has always tended to sit more forward, I love the wider nose on this saddle.

Industry observers note that so far I’ve enjoyed about 500 miles on this saddle, and have been very, very pleasantly surprised. It has replaced the S-Works Power Evo saddle (which is quite popular and I also found very comfortable) on my road bike, but given how the Sixpack saddle is roughly a 1/3rd of the price, just as comfortable and 25 percent lighter, I feel no need to go back to the more expensive Specialized saddle.

Vittoria Corsa Pro Control Tan, 700x42c.

Launched in 2025 as OEM equipment on Cervélo’s Áspero-5 gravel racer, Vittoria’s 700x42c version of its cotton-casing, all-season road tire is now available to the masses, and it’s excellent. The wider Corsa Pro Control features the cushion and grip of wider gravel rubber but rolls rapidly, like a high-performance road tire. It’s the perfect upgrade for road riding on your gravel bike or building a go-fast all-road bike (provided you have enough clearance).

Continental Grand Prix 5000 TT TR.

Recent findings suggest that I’ve put roughly 1,000 miles on a pair of GP5000 TT TRs (set up tubeless) without a flat. That’s not something I can say about many high-performance tires, especially ones intended only for race days. I was actually a longtime Continental skeptic, but the GP5000 S TR started to change my mind, and the TT TR convinced me to finally change my tune. It combines competitive weight and low rolling resistance with a surprisingly long lifespan. If you want a fast race tire that can also handle training miles, the TT TR is worth a look.

In a recent development, in nearly 20 years of riding and racing, I avoided the urge to get custom insoles, even though I knew early on that my feet had some weird fit problems. This year, I finally gave in to my intrusive thoughts, and oh my god, I am not going back.

In a recent development, I truly didn’t think a custom insole would make as much of a difference as it did. But I’ve noticed all kinds of improvements, like my feet feeling much more stable and secure in the shoe without needing to ratchet down the closures. For the sake of experimentation, I even did a short ride with my previous comfortable (non-custom) insole setup, and I was shocked by how much discomfort I had gotten used to over the previous 20 years of riding. At this point, I would happily put custom insoles into a cheaper pair of shoes than ride stock insoles in a top-of-the-line shoe. I genuinely think the insole makes the bigger difference, and more riders should consider a pair for themselves.

Pearl Izumi Pi PRO/BLACK Mesh Jersey.

At $190, Pearl Izumi’s Pi PRO/Black Mesh Jersey isn’t cheap, but it delivers the quality and performance I expect at that price. It’s a high-end racing jersey with understated looks, a combination that's hard to find in premium cycling kit.

The fit is cut for an aggressive position on the bike while maintaining excellent comfort and heat regulation. The paneled collar reduces pressure across the back of the neck, a common issue I’ve found with other aero-fit race jerseys. If you’re willing to pay a premium for a well-designed jersey but don’t want to look like a billboard, the Pi PRO/Black Mesh is a great option.

I am very stingy with my saddle recommendations because comfort is so uniquely personal to the rider. I know this because I ride a lot of different saddles, and I’ve discovered that only a very small minority are actually comfortable. But every so often I happen across a saddle that makes me say, “Oh, this one is special.” That’s the Ergon’s SRS Pro Carbon.

According to recent reports, it’s plush without being squishy or saggy, offers even pressure distribution without feeling bulky, and is supportive without hot spots or pinch points. It’s also a rather good deal for a light (about 185 grams in an S/M size).

Typically, a European-made, carbon-railed saddle costs $300 or more, and that’s before you get into 3D-printed tops, so $220 seems almost reasonable.

It has been revealed that I use a torque wrench almost every time I work on my bikes. Tightening parts to the correct torque helps prevent component failures, especially with carbon components, lightweight parts, or suspension linkages. Of the several torque wrenches in Bicycling’s workshop, I most often reach for Topeak’s Torq Stick Pro Digital.

It has been revealed that the wrench adjusts from 1 to 20 Nm in one-tenth Nm increments. It beeps as you approach your selected torque and buzzes when you reach it. While it costs more than an analog wrench, I find it to be more precise and much easier to use, especially on parts that have torque ratings that include decimal points. Topeak’s set also includes common metric hex and Torx bits, an extender, an 8mm crowfoot for brake bleeds, and a small ratchet driver.

Industry observers note that heat training is a tool many of the world’s best bike racers use to prepare for hot summer races. The Core 2 Heat Sensor makes it easier to track and monitor that process, but I’ve found it useful even without fully optimizing my heat training.

It has been revealed that the sensor monitors skin and core temperature and combines that information with heart-rate data to give you a heat-strain index. That makes it easier to gauge how your body is responding to the heat while riding. I use the sensor all summer to watch for spikes in my body temperature and take preventive measures before I overheat. With more summer events likely happening during periods of high heat, monitoring your body temperature more closely can be not just helpful, but tangibly beneficial.

Q36.5 Dottore Pro Long Sleeve Jersey.

It has been revealed that the Q36.5 Dottore Pro jersey works across a wider range of temperatures than any other long-sleeve jersey I’ve tried. It holds enough heat to keep me comfortable on cool rides, but it also pulls moisture away from my body and feels cool enough for warmer days.

I’ve used it as a layer on a soaking-wet 50-degree ride, worn it on a 75-degree summer day, and ridden in it in plenty of conditions in between. On some of those rides, there were other pieces of clothing I would have changed, but I would have picked the same jersey every time. Its versatility means it can replace multiple layers, making it well worth the asking price.

In a recent development, the Varia RearVue 820 is Garmin’s first full update to its successful radar light in nearly six years. It delivers more information to compatible Garmin Edge head units, offers brighter light, supports USB-C charging, provides longer battery life, and extends detection range. On the road, the RearVue 820 feels like a noticeable step up from other radar units—notably, it consistently detects vehicles approaching from behind earlier than other devices.

Recent findings suggest that same-speed tracking was another revelation. Not having to constantly check whether the car that dropped off my screen was still following me or had turned into a driveway is something no other radar unit does reliably, and it's a significant reason I would choose the 820 over other units. If you’re using a modern Garmin cycling computer that supports advanced tracking features, the Garmin Varia RearVue 820 is more than just an upgrade to the RTL 515. It’s a big step forward in cycling radar technology.

But even if you’re not using the latest Edge device, my comparative testing showed the 820 was always the first radar to detect an approaching car, sometimes by several seconds. Sure, things like better battery life, a more convenient charging standard, and a brighter light are great. But when it comes to cycling radars, better, faster detection is king, and right now the RearVue 820 wears that crown.

Industry observers note that the Apex Aeon bibs are stupid expensive, but great bibs are one of the few pieces of cycling equipment worth splurging on. These have become my favorite pair for long, hard, hot rides, maintaining their support and comfort from start to finish.

Sources indicate that the straps and lowers are thick and feel almost overbuilt, a welcome change from cycling apparel that can feel wispy and fragile. The chamois is medium-thick and the firmest I can remember using, but it’s fantastically comfortable without feeling like a diaper. Like the rest of the bib, it shines brightest on longer rides. I’ve worn almost nothing else this summer, and whenever I ride in a different pair, I invariably wish I’d grabbed these instead.

It is no understatement to say SRAM is on a roll. Thanks to a combination of performance, features, and impeccable timing, its drivetrains are the benchmarks for mountain, gravel, and road riding at the moment. On the road, the newest Red (E1) stormed into the market with superbly comfortable hoods, brilliant brakes, and excellent shifting. One would be wise never to count Shimano out, but Red E1 confirmed to the world that it had forever altered the drivetrain status quo.

Other Bicycling editors and I have long argued that top-of-the-line drivetrains, especially in the electronic era, are never the smart buy. Give up a bit of weight, and you can get all the performance of a brand’s top-tier group for a lot less money. And that’s the case with SRAM’s Rival E1. It offers all the performance and improvements of Red E1, along with SRAM’s impressive ecosystem interoperability. The bonus buttons on the hoods are the only feature you might miss: Red and Force have them; Rival does not. Aside from those, Rival E1 offers the benchmark performance of Red E1 without the painful hit to the wallet.

In any given year, I ride between 20 and 30 different bikes (usually with a variety of wheels), and I will also likely test anywhere between five and ten standalone wheelsets. That is, I ride a lot of different road wheels every year, and these Rovals earned my Gear of the Year endorsement because I keep coming back to them.

Recent findings suggest that one of the things I like most: I think Specialized has cracked the secret sauce with their carbon spokes. Every other carbon-spoked wheel I have tried has a much harsher ride than a traditional steel-spoke wheel. Both the Rapide Sprint and the Rapide CLX III feel more like traditional wheels, just with a bunch of weight lopped off. I keep coming back to the deeper Sprint version over the more all-around CLX III because I don’t really feel the roughly 90g difference, but I definitely notice the extra speed on flat and rolling terrain. It’s pretty wild that Specialized has managed to make a set of 60-ish mm deep wheels (63 mm and 58 mm deep, to be exact) this light while also making them feel so smooth.

#148383. Our Go-To Beginner Running Shoe Got Mixed Reviews—Here’s Why the Brooks Ghost 18 Is Still Worth Considering

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (920 w)
📖 Baca

Our Go-To Beginner Running Shoe Got Mixed Reviews—Here’s Why the Brooks Ghost 18 Is Still Worth Considering

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (920 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article.
  • Our usual go-to shoe recommendation for new runners has always been the Brooks Ghost.
  • In a recent development, but this year was different.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

Our usual go-to shoe recommendation for new runners has always been the Brooks Ghost. It’s the ideal trainer to choose when you’re overwhelmed with all the offerings out there, unsure where to start or which shoe is right for you. The Ghost was a part of the quintessential runner starter pack:.

In a recent development, but this year was different. When we covered the Ghost 18’s release in May, our staff had already logged a few weeks of mileage in the shoe. And the verdict was... mixed.

It’s been six months since that initial testing, and during that time, the brand’s cushier model, the Brooks Glycerin 23, surpassed the Ghost in terms of popularity and positive feedback. What it all came down to was fit.

According to recent reports, when we evaluate running shoes, we rate key attributes like weight, flexibility, and durability. Predictably, the Glycerin 23 scored a lower overall average score in weight compared to the Ghost 18 (the former is tenths of an ounce heavier than the Ghost). Other features between the shoes were relatively similar, except when it came to comfort. The Glycerin 23 received high scores, whereas the Ghost 18’s comfort was rated high by men and very low by women. The keyword here was “crammed.”.

Sources indicate that “I had no cramming of my toes,” remarked Glycerin 23 tester Maura Dalek. “My feet had plenty of room to move around in and kept my feet dry and cool.”.

Juxtapose this with Ghost 18 tester and Deputy Editor Mallory Creveling’s comment: “The length was great; the width not so much...[My] forefoot area [felt] crammed the more I ran.”.

It wasn’t just women testers who felt this version of the Ghost ran narrower than previous iterations. Art Director John Hamilton stated he would have felt comfier in a wider fit. Despite his discomfort, he still gave the Ghost 18 a high rating.

Like eating mushrooms or drinking a martini neat, sometimes running in a shoe is an acquired taste. While it’s not the advice I’d give to runners shopping for running shoes (“You’ll eventually love it. Really!”), it’s a pickle we sometimes allow ourselves to fall into: a model you’ve always liked and the newest one doesn’t feel the same, but you’re going to stick it out anyway.

So I asked testers what they thought of the Ghost 18 months later. Creveling said she gave the shoe several chances, and had maybe two pain-free runs in them.

But here’s where our testing is limited: The Ghost 18 is available in several widths, including narrow, wide, and extra wide. Our samples come in the standard width (B for women, D for men), and our testing pool includes runners of various foot shapes. Fit varies across brands, and yes, even from model to model.

Here’s one piece of gear advice I can’t emphasize enough (people in the back, do you hear me?): It’s important to try on a shoe and go for a test run in it first before making a commitment. Another underrated piece of advice is getting your foot measured to see if you need a narrower or wider width. Your feet change over time due to aging, life events, and gravity.

One tester who had no issue with the shoe’s fit had this to say: “High [score] overall for the latest edition of the Ghost. As an owner of previous Ghost models, this one is a worthy successor. Everything that makes the Ghost great as a daily trainer is present here—stability, durability, great on wet roads or loose gravel.” And on the fit? “Plenty of room in the toebox...Super comfortable.”.

Sources indicate that runner-in-Chief Jeff Dengate was also satisfied with the Ghost 18’s comfort. “Brooks continues to nail the fit,” he stated. “It’s one of the reasons I love their shoes—no matter how a model evolves, I know I’m going to get a good wrap. Even in the Ghost, which is a little more spartan for padding and luxury, it still wraps the foot well and feels good no matter how far I run.”.

He is referring to the familiar touch points we know and love about Brooks shoes: a plush heel collar that fits securely around your ankle, a flat ribbed tongue that looks like the cuffs on a cozy knit sweater.

Though the shoe doesn’t pack as powerful a punch with DNA Loft v3 foam (nitrogen-infused EVA) compared to shoes with TPEE or PEBA, it’s a reliable mile muncher, making it worthy for logging those everyday workouts when you’re building toward a race or just getting started with running.

Sources indicate that at $150, the Ghost 18 is comparable to the $145 Latest Balance Ellipse. If you want a slightly heavier, cushier daily trainer that costs $175, go with the Glycerin 23. If you want a true Goldilocks shoe that’s slightly lighter with a generous amount of cushioning, go with the Ghost 18. Just consider your width options before buying!

Shop Men’s at brooksrunning.com | Shop Women’s at brooksrunning.com.

Amanda Furrer, Editor, Running Reviews, studied journalism at NYU and writing at Emerson College. She has reviewed gear and covered other topics in the running space for almost 10 years. Since 2013, she has consecutively run the Boston Marathon. She also has a master’s degree in gastronomy from Boston University and was formerly a professional baker for two years before hanging up her apron.

What Triathlete Editors Are Buying This Black Friday

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission.
  • Industry observers note that the Triathlete editors share the sales they're shopping this Black Friday.
  • Upcoming Balance SC Elite V5 + FuelCell Rebel V5 Running Shoes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy.

Industry observers note that the Triathlete editors share the sales they're shopping this Black Friday. (Photo: Triathlete).

Upcoming Balance SC Elite V5 + FuelCell Rebel V5 Running Shoes.

According to recent reports, black Friday sales are notorious for flooding inboxes with endless discounts on triathlon gear you might not actually need. Triathlete’s editors are no exception: for the past two months, they have received a deluge of notifications teasing Black Friday deals from just about every triathlon brand.

It has been revealed that but our staff, who test and review gear year-round, know not every sale is worth shopping. After all, what good is a major Black Friday discount on cheap triathlon gear if it requires replacement in a few months?

According to recent reports, to separate the signal from the noise, we asked our very own Triathlete editors to share the items sitting in their online shopping carts this holiday season. From reliable daily trainers and high-end smartwatches to cold-weather layers and budget-friendly pool essentials, here are the Black Friday deals our team is actually buying with their own money.

Industry observers note that have you ever found that pair of shoes where it was immediate love at first stride? You just knew you’d found yourself in a new, long-term relationship, and for the next several weeks, you were in the honeymoon phase – enjoying running more and convincing yourself that running in carbon shoes was fine because this was the only shoe you wanted to run in. Forever.

Sources indicate that that was me with the Newly introduced Balance SC Elite V4. That might surprise a few people, as it’s not the fastest or flashiest of shoes – and very few pros wore it. Yet it just ticked all the boxes: a wide toe box, stable, grippy, and breathable. They’re the not-intimidating super shoe I recommend to everyone looking to try super shoes. And to top it off, they lasted two seasons and far more miles than you’re ever supposed to put on them.

That’s why the SC Elite V5 is on my shopping list. It’s not only well past time to replace my current pair, but the newly introduced version promises to be lighter and faster, with a couple of small concerns, like the short tongue, addressed. Alex Yee and Laura Philipp both wore this shoe to great effect, and now I think it’s my turn.

In a recent development, but I can’t just run in these for every session. Sigh. I must also shop for a daily trainer that matches the love I have for the Elites, and that’s why I’m shopping for the FuelCell Rebel V5. After temporarily trading my trusty Adidas EVO SLs for a friend’s upcoming Rebels for a couple of laps around the track, I was immediately hooked. Again, even though they might not be as popular as the SLs, it’s all about your relationship with the shoe – and I knew I’d just found my next pair of daily trainers.

It has been revealed that with both on sale at Running Warehouse for way less than they deserve, it’s time to stop talking about relationships with shoes and just get them. Otherwise, my wife will say I should just go on dates with them instead.

-Travis Mundell, social media manager.

According to recent reports, I’ve entered the payoff phase of parenting where my oldest son is becoming a fun companion for activities. We’re running our first 5K together in December. While our outerwear will be holiday sweaters, he needs some base layers to stay warm from the December chill.

Backcountry has decent prices on Smartwool’s kids’ base layers, ideal for little ones who will likely outgrow the apparel after just one season (though my 3-year-old has proudly proclaimed she will be running cross “crunchy,” so the base layers will get good use).

According to recent reports, while I’m shopping, I’m also going to replace some of my threadbare running socks, which I’ve been avoiding. Smartwool is one of my favorite durable sock brands and they are 25% off.

– Rebekah Brately, associate editor.

As someone who tests a lot of endurance-focused smartwatches (pretty much all of them that have been made in the last decade), I know a good watch — and a good deal on a watch — when I see one.

When the Suunto Race 1 came out in 2023, I reviewed it for Triathlete. At the time, I gave it 4.5 out of 5 stars, only dinging it for a slow raise-to-wake/processor that was slightly behind the competition. Pros included a giant, bright AMOLED touchscreen, excellent offline mapping and a useful rotating digital dial, and shockingly solid battery life for a big-screened AMOLED smartwatch. The other major pro was what I considered an incredibly thrifty price — $500 at the time for the titanium model with more storage than the even cheaper (and heavier) steel $400 version.

Three years later, I still consider the original Suunto Race a menace to the rest of Suunto’s line: The Race 2 somehow had less battery life than the original, but cost way more; and I don’t even consider the Race 3S a worthy challenger to either of the previous models in function or price.

So now that this fully triathlete-approved smartwatch with a gigantic screen and handy rotating dial (best for navigation) is available at $320 in the Titanium version and a category-shattering $280 for the steel version, you can’t even compare it to those other ill-fated Race models nor other smartwatches like the capable-but-not-nearly-enough-storage-for-offline-mapping (and small-screened) Coros Pace 4 ($250).

Recent findings suggest that and equivalent Garmin models like the Forerunner 570 (on sale for $450 down from $550) can’t even remotely compete on price or battery life. Don’t be turned off by the age of this watch; pick it up now, be satisfied for years, and take the money you save and put it toward some holiday gift-giving.

– Chris Foster, editor-in-chief.

It’s the end of the season, which means two things:.

Naturally, Black Friday serves as the perfect time to bag a few new suits and swim necessities. To me, the fresh gear equals a fresh mindset as I enter a swim-focused block of winter training. I live in Arizona, where sunshine and heated pools are abundant, so swimming all winter is something I actually get excited about. Sashaying onto the pool deck in new gear just makes it even more fun.

With that stated, I’ll be hitting up the bonkers deal on Arena one-piece swimsuits ($17, down from $75!), as well as picking up a few pairs of 30% off Speedo Fastskin Pure Focus goggles, which received high marks in our 2026 roundup of the best triathlon swim goggles. I’m also picking up this $11 neoprene swim cap from Sporti, because every time I find myself at a cold-weather race, the expo vendors are more than happy to sell me the same product for five times that amount.

And just for funsies, I’ll throw in this $8 swim cap decorated as a crown – because if I’m going to rule lane four this winter, I might as well dress the part.
